lessons.title: Why Object Oriented Programming?
lessons.content:
Imagine you are building a game of cricket on a computer. There are players, a bat, a ball, a pitch, two umpires and a scoreboard. Each of these things has some information about itself, and each can do something. A batter has a name, runs and balls faced, and can hit the ball. The scoreboard has the total and wickets, and it can update itself. If you write your program the same way, as a small world of things that each know their own data and their own jobs, you are doing Object Oriented Programming, or OOP.

What OOP is: Object Oriented Programming is a way of designing programs around objects. An object is a bundle of two things: data (what it has) and behaviour (what it can do). The data is stored in variables called fields or attributes, and the behaviour is written as functions called methods. Objects are made from classes, and a class is like a blueprint or a cookie cutter. One class, many objects. This course teaches you how to think in objects and how to write them in real languages, mostly Java, with a look at C++ near the end.

The old way, procedural programming: Before OOP became popular, most programs were written in a procedural style, like in C. You think of the program as a list of steps and you split it into functions. The data usually lives separately, often in global variables or structures, and any function can reach in and change it. For small programs this works fine. Your first course in C was probably procedural: read numbers, loop, calculate, print.

Where procedural code starts to hurt: Now imagine a bank program with 200,000 lines of C. The account balance is a plain variable that 300 different functions can touch. One day the balance becomes negative by mistake. Which of the 300 functions did it? You have to search them all. Also, if you change how the balance is stored, for example from int to a structure with currency, every one of those functions may break. The data and the code that works on it are far apart, so the program becomes hard to understand, hard to change and easy to break.

The object oriented idea: OOP says, keep the data and the code that works on that data together, in one unit, and let only that unit change the data. The balance lives inside an Account object, and the only way to change it is to call deposit() or withdraw() on that account. Those methods check the rules. Now if the balance goes wrong, you know exactly where to look: inside the Account class. This simple change, putting data and behaviour together and guarding the data, makes huge programs much easier to manage.

A tiny comparison: In a procedural style you might write withdraw(balance, 500), passing the data to a function. In OOP style you write myAccount.withdraw(500), asking the object to do something to itself. It looks like a small change in syntax, but it is a big change in thinking. You stop asking "what steps should run?" and start asking "what things exist, what do they know, and what can they do?"

A short history: The ideas of OOP are older than most people think. In the 1960s, two Norwegian researchers, Ole-Johan Dahl and Kristen Nygaard, created a language called Simula for writing simulations, and it introduced classes and objects. In the 1970s, Alan Kay and his team at Xerox PARC built Smalltalk, where everything was an object, and Alan Kay is often credited with the term "object oriented". In the 1980s, Bjarne Stroustrup added classes to C and the result became C++. In 1995, Sun Microsystems released Java, designed by James Gosling's team, which made OOP mainstream. Today Python, C#, Kotlin, Swift, Dart and many more languages support OOP.

Objects in the real world: Look around your room. A fan has a speed level and it can turn on, turn off and change speed. A mobile phone has a battery level, a number and contacts, and it can call, send SMS and take photos. A rickshaw has a driver, a fare and a location, and it can move and stop. Every real thing has state (its current data) and behaviour (what it can do). OOP copies this pattern into code, so programs feel closer to the problem you are solving.

State, behaviour and identity: Three words describe any object. State is the current values of its fields, like a fan at speed 3. Behaviour is the set of methods it offers, like turnOn(). Identity means each object is its own separate thing, even if two objects have the same values. Two fans can both be at speed 3, but they are still two different fans. Switching off one does not switch off the other. Keep these three words in mind; exams often ask for them.

Class versus object: A class is the design; an object is a real thing built from it. Think of the design of a Walton fridge model in a factory. The design itself does not keep anything cold. The fridges built from that design are real, each in a different home, each with different food inside. In code, Student is a class, and rahim and fatima are objects of the Student class, each with its own name and roll number. We say each object is an instance of the class.

A first look in Java: Here is a very small class. class Fan { int speed; void turnOn() { speed = 1; } } Then in main we write: Fan f = new Fan(); f.turnOn(); The class Fan says every fan has a speed and can turn on. The keyword new builds a real fan object in memory, and f.turnOn() asks that object to run its method. Do not worry about every detail now; lessons 3 to 6 go through it slowly.

The four pillars, a preview: OOP is usually described with four big ideas, called the four pillars. You will hear them in every exam and every job interview, so meet them now. Each one gets its own lessons later in the course.

Pillar 1, Encapsulation: Encapsulation means wrapping data and methods together in a class, and hiding the data so outsiders cannot change it directly. Like a medicine capsule, the inside is protected. A bank account keeps its balance private and offers safe methods to change it. Lesson 7 covers this in depth.

Pillar 2, Abstraction: Abstraction means showing only the important features and hiding the complicated details. When you ride a motorbike you use the throttle and brake, but you do not need to know how fuel burns inside the engine. In code, abstract classes and interfaces describe what something can do without saying how. Lessons 13 and 14 cover this.

Pillar 3, Inheritance: Inheritance lets a new class reuse an existing class and add to it. A CSEStudent class can inherit name and roll from a Student class and add a favourite programming language. This creates an "is-a" relationship: a CSE student is a student. Lessons 10 and 11 cover this.

Pillar 4, Polymorphism: Polymorphism means "many forms": one method name, many behaviours. You can ask every animal to makeSound(), and a cat meows while a dog barks. Your code just says makeSound() and the right version runs. Lesson 12 covers this.

Benefits of OOP: Modularity, because each class is a separate piece you can understand alone. Reusability, because a well written class can be used in many programs, and inheritance lets you build on it. Easier maintenance, because a bug in account rules lives in one class. Security of data, because private fields cannot be changed from outside. Better modelling, because classes match real things like Student, Course and Teacher, so teams can talk about the design easily.

Drawbacks of OOP: OOP is not magic. Programs can become larger, with many small classes. Beginners sometimes create too many classes or deep inheritance chains that are hard to follow. Some kinds of programs, like a short script that renames files or heavy number crunching, can be simpler in a procedural or functional style. Good programmers choose the style that fits the problem, and many modern languages mix styles.

Real life example 1, a Pathao or Uber style ride app: Think about the things in the system. There is a Rider with a name, phone and rating. There is a Driver with a name, vehicle and current location. There is a Ride with pickup point, drop point, distance and fare. The Ride can calculateFare() and the Driver can acceptRide(). A bike ride and a car ride calculate fare differently but both answer calculateFare(). Here you can already see classes, objects, encapsulation (the fare is changed only through methods) and polymorphism working together.

Real life example 2, a school result system: A school in Dhaka wants to manage results. Classes could be Student, Teacher, Subject and ResultSheet. A Student object knows its name, class and roll. A ResultSheet object holds marks and can calculateGPA(). A Teacher can enterMarks(). If the GPA rules change next year, only the calculateGPA() method needs to change. Nothing else in the system breaks, because nothing else touches the GPA calculation directly.

Languages you will use: Java is the main language in many Bangladeshi universities for this course because it is purely class based (every function lives inside a class) and has good error messages. C++ is also common, especially in BUET and KUET style syllabuses, because it lets you see memory, destructors and operator overloading. Python supports OOP too, but its rules are looser. The ideas are the same in all of them; only the syntax changes.

Common mistakes: Students often think OOP just means "using classes". You can put all your code into one giant class and still write procedural code. OOP means designing with objects that own their data and responsibilities. Another mistake is mixing up class and object: the class is the blueprint, the object is the real thing. A third mistake is mixing up encapsulation and abstraction. Encapsulation is about protecting data by bundling and hiding it; abstraction is about hiding complexity and showing only what matters.

What exams ask: Typical questions are "Define OOP and compare it with procedural programming", "What are the four pillars of OOP? Explain each with an example", "Differentiate between class and object", and "What are the advantages of OOP?". A short comparison table (procedural: functions first, data shared, top-down; OOP: objects first, data hidden, bottom-up) earns good marks.

Recap: OOP organises a program as a set of objects, each with state, behaviour and identity, built from classes. It grew from Simula and Smalltalk into C++ and Java. Its four pillars are encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance and polymorphism. Next lesson we will quickly refresh the Java basics you need, so that from lesson 3 onwards we can build real classes and objects.
key_points: OOP organises a program around objects that bundle data (fields) and behaviour (methods).
A class is a blueprint; an object is an instance built from it.
Every object has state, behaviour and identity.
Procedural code separates data and functions; OOP keeps them together and guards the data.
OOP grew from Simula (1960s) and Smalltalk (1970s) into C++ and Java (1995).
The four pillars: encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism.
OOP gives modularity, reuse and easier maintenance, but can add size and complexity.
lessons.tip: For every new topic, pick one real object around you (fan, phone, rickshaw) and say its state and behaviour out loud. It trains your OOP eye fast.
lessons.task: On paper, list 3 objects from a cricket match. For each write 3 fields (state) and 2 methods (behaviour), e.g. Batter: name, runs, balls; hit(), getOut().

lessons.title: Java Essentials for OOP
lessons.content:
Before you can build objects, you need to be comfortable with the language you will build them in. Think of it like cricket: before learning clever field placements, you must be able to catch and throw. This lesson is a quick, friendly tour of the Java basics you need for the rest of the course. If you already know C, you will find that most of it looks familiar, with a few important differences.

Why Java for OOP: Java was designed from the start as an object oriented language. Every piece of code in Java lives inside a class, so you cannot avoid thinking in classes. It also has automatic memory management, clear error messages and a huge standard library. Android apps were traditionally written in Java, many bank and enterprise systems use it, and many Bangladeshi universities teach the OOP course with it.

JDK, JRE and JVM: These three names confuse everyone at first. The JVM (Java Virtual Machine) is the program that actually runs Java code. The JRE (Java Runtime Environment) is the JVM plus the standard libraries, which is what you need to run Java programs. The JDK (Java Development Kit) is the JRE plus developer tools such as the compiler javac, which is what you need to write programs. A simple memory trick: JDK contains JRE, and JRE contains JVM.

Bytecode and "write once, run anywhere": In C, the compiler turns your code into machine code for one kind of processor and operating system. Java does it differently. The javac compiler turns Hello.java into Hello.class, which contains bytecode, a set of instructions for the JVM, not for a real chip. Then the JVM on each machine runs that bytecode. Windows, Linux and macOS each have their own JVM, so the same .class file runs on all of them. That is the meaning of Java's slogan "write once, run anywhere". Modern JVMs also use a JIT (just-in-time) compiler that turns frequently used bytecode into fast machine code while the program runs.

Your first program: Every Java program starts from a main method inside a class. public class Hello { public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("Assalamu alaikum, Java!"); } } Save it as Hello.java, because a public class must be in a file with the same name. Compile with javac Hello.java and run with java Hello. The word public means anyone can call it, static means it belongs to the class so Java can call it without creating an object, void means it returns nothing, and String[] args holds any command line arguments. You will understand each of those words properly by lesson 7.

Printing and comments: System.out.println prints and moves to a new line, System.out.print prints without a new line, and System.out.printf works like printf in C, for example System.out.printf("%.2f", 3.14159) prints 3.14. Comments are written with // for one line and /* ... */ for many lines. Java also has /** ... */ documentation comments, which the javadoc tool can turn into web pages.

Primitive data types: Java has exactly eight primitive types. Four for whole numbers: byte (8 bits), short (16 bits), int (32 bits) and long (64 bits). Two for decimals: float (32 bits) and double (64 bits). One for a single character: char, which is 16 bits and stores a Unicode character, so it can hold a Bangla letter. And boolean, which is only true or false. Unlike C, the sizes are fixed on every machine, and a boolean is not a number: you cannot write if (1) in Java.

Literals and defaults: A whole number like 25 is an int by default, and a decimal like 3.5 is a double by default. To make a long you add L, as in 8000000000L, and to make a float you add f, as in 2.5f. Characters use single quotes, 'A', and strings use double quotes, "Dhaka". Inside a method, local variables must be given a value before use; the compiler refuses to compile int x; System.out.println(x);. This protects you from the garbage values you may have seen in C.

Type conversion and casting: Java converts automatically from a smaller type to a larger one, called widening: int a = 10; double d = a; is fine and d becomes 10.0. Going from larger to smaller, called narrowing, needs an explicit cast because you may lose data: double price = 99.75; int taka = (int) price; gives 99, because the decimal part is cut off, not rounded. Integer division also cuts: 7 / 2 is 3, while 7 / 2.0 is 3.5.

Operators: Arithmetic operators are + - * / and % (remainder, so 17 % 5 is 2). Comparison operators are == != < > <= >= and they produce a boolean. Logical operators are && (and), || (or) and ! (not). && and || are short-circuit: in (x != 0 && 10 / x > 1), if x is 0 the second part is never checked, so there is no division by zero. Increment ++ and decrement -- work like in C, and compound operators like += save typing. The + operator also joins strings: "Roll: " + 42 gives "Roll: 42".

Control flow: if, else if and else work exactly like C. The switch statement works on int, char, String and enums; with the classic form you must remember break, or execution falls through to the next case. Newer Java versions also have an arrow form, case 1 -> System.out.println("One");, that does not fall through. Loops are the familiar for, while and do-while, plus break to leave a loop and continue to skip to the next round.

The enhanced for loop: Java adds a cleaner loop for going through every element of an array or collection. int[] marks = {78, 85, 91}; for (int m : marks) { System.out.println(m); } Read the colon as "in": for each m in marks. You cannot change the array's elements through m, and you do not get the index, but for simple reading it is short and safe.

Arrays in Java: Arrays are objects in Java. You create one with new: int[] runs = new int[5]; makes five ints, all starting at 0. You can also write int[] runs = {4, 6, 0, 1, 2};. Every array knows its own size through runs.length (no brackets, it is a field, not a method). If you try runs[5], Java does not silently read garbage memory like C; it throws an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException and stops. This bounds checking is one of Java's big safety features.

Two-dimensional arrays: int[][] board = new int[3][3]; makes a 3 by 3 grid, handy for tic-tac-toe. Java actually makes an array of arrays, so rows can even have different lengths, called a jagged array: int[][] t = new int[3][]; t[0] = new int[2]; t[1] = new int[5];. board.length gives the number of rows, and board[0].length gives the length of the first row.

Reading input with Scanner: To read from the keyboard you usually use the Scanner class. import java.util.Scanner; then Scanner sc = new Scanner(System.in); int n = sc.nextInt(); String name = sc.next(); String line = sc.nextLine();. A classic beginner trap: after nextInt(), the Enter key is still waiting in the input, so a following nextLine() reads an empty line. The fix is to call an extra sc.nextLine() to throw it away.

Strings, a first look: String is not a primitive; it is a class, but Java gives it special support so you can write String city = "Sylhet";. city.length() gives 6, city.charAt(0) gives 'S', and city.toUpperCase() gives "SYLHET". Very important: compare strings with city.equals("Sylhet"), not with ==. Lesson 8 explains exactly why.

Methods, a first look: A function in Java is called a method and must be inside a class. static int square(int x) { return x * x; } can be called from main as square(5), which returns 25. We mark it static here because main is static and we have no object yet. From lesson 3 onwards we will write non-static methods that belong to objects, which is the real OOP way.

Naming conventions: Java programmers follow strong naming habits, and examiners notice them. Class names use PascalCase: Student, BankAccount. Methods and variables use camelCase: getName, totalMarks. Constants use UPPER_SNAKE_CASE: MAX_SPEED. Package names are all lowercase. Following these makes your code look professional immediately.

The Math class: Java gives you ready-made maths in the Math class, so you do not need to write it yourself. Math.sqrt(49) gives 7.0, Math.pow(2, 10) gives 1024.0, Math.abs(-5) gives 5, Math.max(3, 9) gives 9 and Math.round(2.5) gives 3. Math.random() gives a double from 0.0 up to but not including 1.0, so (int)(Math.random() * 6) + 1 simulates a dice roll from 1 to 6. Notice that we call these methods on the class name, not on an object; they are static methods, which lesson 6 explains.

Constants with final: If a value should never change, mark it final: final double VAT_RATE = 0.15;. Any later line that tries VAT_RATE = 0.2; will not compile. Constants make code easier to read, because a name like VAT_RATE says much more than a bare 0.15 hidden in a formula, and if the rate changes you edit it in one place. Lesson 6 shows how final also works with methods and classes.

Real life example 1, a cricket scorecard: Store the runs of each over in an array: int[] overs = {6, 4, 10, 2, 8};. Use an enhanced for loop to add them: int total = 0; for (int r : overs) total += r;. The total is 30. The run rate is (double) total / overs.length, which gives 6.0; without the cast, integer division could cut off decimals for other totals. Print it with printf("%.2f", rate).

Real life example 2, a bKash style balance check: Read an amount with Scanner, check it with if: if (amount <= 0) print "Invalid amount"; else if (amount > balance) print "Insufficient balance"; else subtract it. Notice how the data (balance) and the rules (the if checks) are still separate here. In lesson 7 we will move them into an Account class, which is exactly the OOP improvement.

Common mistakes: Naming the file differently from the public class. Using == for strings. Forgetting that 7 / 2 is 3. Forgetting break in a classic switch. Reading past the end of an array. The nextInt() then nextLine() trap. Writing if (x = 5) instead of if (x == 5); in Java this does not even compile for an int, which is helpful.

What exams ask: "Differentiate between JDK, JRE and JVM", "What is bytecode and why is Java platform independent?", "List the primitive data types of Java with their sizes", "Explain widening and narrowing conversion with examples" and short code tracing questions with integer division and loops.

Recap: Java source is compiled to bytecode and run by the JVM, which makes it portable. It has eight primitive types with fixed sizes, C-like operators and loops, safe arrays with a length field, and the Scanner class for input. With these basics ready, the next lesson finally opens the real heart of OOP: classes and objects.
key_points: JDK contains JRE, and JRE contains the JVM that runs bytecode.
javac compiles .java into bytecode (.class); the JVM on each OS runs it, so Java is portable.
Java has 8 primitive types with fixed sizes; char is 16-bit Unicode and boolean is not a number.
Widening is automatic; narrowing needs a cast and may lose data (int)99.75 is 99.
Arrays are objects with a length field and bounds checking.
Scanner reads input; beware the nextInt() then nextLine() trap.
Compare strings with equals(), not ==.
lessons.tip: Type and run every small example yourself. Making the compiler complain and then fixing it teaches Java faster than reading.
lessons.task: Write a Java program that stores 6 over-by-over run totals in an array, prints the total with an enhanced for loop, and prints the run rate with 2 decimals.

quiz.q: Which of these contains the compiler javac?
quiz.explain: The JDK is JRE plus development tools like javac.

quiz.q: What does int taka = (int) 99.75; store?
quiz.explain: Casting double to int cuts off the decimal part, it does not round.

quiz.q: Why is Java called platform independent?
options: Bytecode is run by a JVM available on each platform
quiz.explain: The same bytecode runs on any machine that has a JVM.

quiz.q: How many primitive data types does Java have?
quiz.explain: byte, short, int, long, float, double, char and boolean.

quiz.q: What happens when you access runs[5] in an array of length 5?
quiz.explain: Java checks bounds; valid indexes are 0 to 4.

lessons.title: Classes and Objects
lessons.content:
Think about a tailor in Dhaka's New Market. He has one paper pattern for a shirt: where the collar goes, how long the sleeves are, how many buttons. From that single pattern he can cut fifty shirts, in different colours and sizes, for fifty different customers. The pattern itself is not a shirt; you cannot wear it. The shirts are real. In OOP, the pattern is a class and each shirt is an object. This lesson is about that idea in full detail, because everything else in the course is built on it.

What a class is: A class is a user-defined type that describes what data its objects will hold and what they can do. It is a plan, written once. In Java you write it with the keyword class followed by a name in PascalCase and a pair of braces. Inside the braces you put the members of the class: fields (variables) and methods (functions). A class takes no space for object data until you actually create an object from it.

What an object is: An object is a real instance of a class, created while the program runs. It has its own copy of every instance field, so changing one object's data does not touch another object's data. If Student is the class, then the student called Rahim with roll 101 and the student called Fatima with roll 102 are two objects. We often say "Rahim is an instance of Student".

Your first real class: class Student { String name; int roll; double cgpa; void introduce() { System.out.println("I am " + name + ", roll " + roll); } } This class has three fields, name, roll and cgpa, and one method, introduce(). Notice the method uses name and roll directly; inside a class, methods can freely use the object's own fields.

Creating an object with new: In main you write Student s1 = new Student();. Three things happen here. First, Student s1 declares a reference variable called s1 that can point to a Student. Second, new Student() asks Java to make a fresh object in memory, with space for name, roll and cgpa. Third, the = stores the address of that new object in s1. After this line, s1 refers to a real student object.

Using the dot operator: To reach an object's members you use a dot. s1.name = "Rahim"; s1.roll = 101; s1.introduce(); prints "I am Rahim, roll 101". Read s1.introduce() as "hey s1, introduce yourself". Later, in lesson 7, we will make the fields private so outsiders cannot write s1.roll = -5, but for now direct access helps you see what is going on.

Default values of fields: If you create an object and do not set its fields, Java gives them default values. Numbers become 0 (or 0.0), boolean becomes false, char becomes the null character, and any reference such as a String becomes null. So a new Student has name null, roll 0 and cgpa 0.0. This is different from local variables inside methods, which get no default and must be set before use.

Many objects from one class: Student s2 = new Student(); s2.name = "Fatima"; s2.roll = 102;. Now there are two separate objects. If you change s1.cgpa = 3.75, s2.cgpa stays 0.0. Each object carries its own state. This is how one class can model a whole classroom of 60 students: one blueprint, 60 objects.

References, not objects, live in variables: This is the most important idea of the lesson. A variable like s1 does not contain the object; it contains a reference, which you can think of as the address of the object, like a house address written on a card. The object itself lives somewhere else in memory. When you print a reference directly, System.out.println(s1), Java prints something like Student@1b6d3586, which is the class name and a hash code, not the data. Lesson 15 shows how to fix this with toString().

Stack and heap: Java memory is roughly split into two areas you should know. The stack holds method calls and their local variables, including reference variables like s1. Each method call gets its own stack frame, which disappears when the method returns. The heap holds all objects created with new. So in Student s1 = new Student();, the variable s1 sits on the stack, and the Student object with its name, roll and cgpa sits on the heap. The arrow from s1 to the object is the reference.

Copying a reference: Student s3 = s1; does not create a new student. It copies the address, so s1 and s3 now point to the same object. If you write s3.name = "Rahim Uddin";, then s1.name also shows "Rahim Uddin", because it is the very same object. Two cards, one house. This surprises almost every beginner, so trace it on paper with boxes and arrows.

null and NullPointerException: A reference can point to nothing; then its value is null. Student s4 = null; is legal. But s4.introduce() will crash with a NullPointerException, because there is no object to ask. This is one of the most common runtime errors in Java. Before using a reference that might be null, check it: if (s4 != null) s4.introduce();.

Object identity versus equal content: s1 == s3 is true, because both references point to the same object. But if you create Student a = new Student(); a.name = "Rahim"; and Student b = new Student(); b.name = "Rahim";, then a == b is false. They have the same content but they are two different objects with two different addresses. == on references compares identity, not content. Comparing content needs an equals() method, covered in lesson 15.

Instance methods use the object's own data: Add a method to Student: void addMarks(double gp) { cgpa = (cgpa + gp) / 2; }. When you call s1.addMarks(4.0), the method works on s1's cgpa. When you call s2.addMarks(3.0), it works on s2's cgpa. The same code, different data, decided by which object you called it on. Java secretly passes the calling object to the method; inside, you can name it with the keyword this, which lesson 6 explores.

Garbage, and who cleans it: If you write s1 = new Student(); again, the first Student object no longer has any reference pointing to it. It is unreachable, like a house nobody has the address of. Java's garbage collector will eventually find such objects and free their memory automatically. You never call free() as in C. Lesson 5 says a bit more about object lifetime.

Arrays of objects: You can make an array of references: Student[] batch = new Student[3];. Careful: this creates three references, all null, not three students. You still need batch[0] = new Student(); and so on, usually in a loop. Forgetting this and calling batch[0].introduce() gives a NullPointerException. Lesson 9 uses arrays of objects heavily.

Designing a good class: A class should represent one clear idea, and its name should be a noun: Book, Account, Ride. Fields describe what every object of that kind has; methods describe what it can do, usually named with verbs: borrow(), deposit(), calculateFare(). A good test is to say the sentence "A Book has a title and an author and can be borrowed." If the sentence sounds strange, the design probably is.

UML class box, a first look: Designers draw a class as a box with three parts: the class name on top, fields in the middle, and methods at the bottom. For Student: name, roll, cgpa in the middle; introduce() and addMarks() at the bottom. Exams often ask you to draw this. Lesson 25 covers UML properly, with symbols for private and public.

Members of a class, a full list: So far we have fields and methods, but a Java class can contain a few more kinds of members. Constructors, which set up a new object (lesson 5). Static fields and methods, which belong to the class as a whole rather than to one object (lesson 6). Initializer blocks, which run code while an object is being built. And nested classes, which are classes written inside another class. You will meet each one in time; for now, remember that fields hold state and methods hold behaviour.

Where to put classes: A Java file can hold several classes, but at most one of them can be public, and that public class must match the file name. Beginners often write class Student and class Main in the same file Main.java, with only Main public, and that works. In bigger projects each class usually gets its own file, such as Student.java and Book.java, which keeps things tidy and easy to find.

A worked trace: Consider this code. Student a = new Student(); a.roll = 1; Student b = new Student(); b.roll = 2; Student c = a; c.roll = 5; a = b; System.out.println(a.roll + " " + c.roll);. Let us trace it. Object X is created with roll 1 and a points to it. Object Y is created with roll 2 and b points to it. c copies a's address, so c points to X. c.roll = 5 changes X's roll to 5. Then a = b makes a point to Y. Now a.roll is Y's roll, 2, and c.roll is X's roll, 5. The output is "2 5". Notice that X is still alive, because c still points to it.

Why the heap at all: You might wonder why objects do not simply live on the stack like local ints. The reason is lifetime. A stack frame vanishes when its method returns, but an object often needs to live longer, for example a Student created inside a helper method and returned to main, or a Book stored in a library list for the whole program. The heap lets objects outlive the method that created them, and the garbage collector removes them only when nobody can reach them any more.

Real life example 1, a library: Class Book with fields title, author, isBorrowed, and methods borrow() and giveBack(). In main, Book b1 = new Book(); b1.title = "Himu"; b1.author = "Humayun Ahmed"; then b1.borrow(); sets isBorrowed to true. A second Book object for another title stays unaffected. If two variables point to the same book and one of them borrows it, the other sees it borrowed too, exactly like two library cards pointing to one physical book.

Real life example 2, a mobile phone: Class Phone with fields owner, battery and balance, and methods call(minutes) and charge(). Phone p = new Phone(); p.battery = 40; p.call(10); could reduce battery by 2 per minute, making it 20. Your friend's phone object has its own battery. Each Phone object is like a real handset in someone's pocket: same model design, different state.

Common mistakes: Thinking Student s; creates an object (it only declares a reference). Forgetting new in arrays of objects. Expecting Student s3 = s1; to copy the student. Using == to compare object content. Calling a method on a null reference. Printing an object and expecting to see its fields.

What exams ask: "Define class and object with an example", "What is the difference between a class and an object?", "Explain how objects are created in Java using new", "What is a reference variable?", tracing questions where two references point to one object, and "Draw the memory diagram (stack and heap) for the following code".

Recap: A class is a blueprint that defines fields and methods; an object is an instance with its own state, created on the heap with new. Variables hold references, not objects, so copying a variable copies the address. == compares identity, null means no object, and unreachable objects are cleaned up by the garbage collector. Next we look closer at methods: parameters, return values and overloading.
key_points: A class is a blueprint of fields and methods; an object is a real instance with its own state.
new creates an object on the heap and returns a reference to it.
Reference variables hold addresses; Student s3 = s1 makes two names for one object.
Fields get default values (0, false, null); local variables do not.
== on references compares identity, not content.
Calling a method on null throws NullPointerException.
new Student[3] creates 3 null references, not 3 students.
Unreachable objects are freed by the garbage collector.
lessons.tip: Draw boxes and arrows for every object example: a box on the stack for the variable, a box on the heap for the object, an arrow between. Most reference bugs vanish once you draw them.
lessons.task: Write a Book class with title, author and isBorrowed plus borrow(). In main create two books, make a third variable point to the first, borrow through it, and print both books' isBorrowed to see the shared object.

quiz.q: What does Student s; alone do?
options: Declares a reference that does not yet point to an object
quiz.explain: Only new creates an object; this line just declares a reference variable.

quiz.q: Where are objects created with new stored?
quiz.explain: Objects live on the heap; local reference variables live on the stack.

quiz.q: After Student b = a; b.name = 'X';, what is a.name?
quiz.explain: a and b refer to the same object, so the change is visible through both.

quiz.q: What is the default value of an int field in a new object?
quiz.explain: Numeric fields default to 0.

quiz.q: Which error comes from calling a method on a reference whose value is null?
quiz.explain: There is no object to run the method on.

lessons.title: Methods in Depth
lessons.content:
Think of a tea stall at the corner of your street. You say "one milk tea, less sugar" and hand over 15 taka. The tea seller does a fixed set of steps, and hands you back a cup of tea. You gave him inputs (your order and money), he did some work, and he returned an output (the tea). You do not need to know how he boils the water. A method in Java works the same way: it takes inputs called parameters, does some work, and may return a result. In OOP, methods are how objects do things, so it is worth learning them properly.

What a method is: A method is a named block of code inside a class that performs one task. It has a header and a body. The header, also called the signature plus return type, looks like this: double calculateFare(double km, boolean isAC). Here double is the return type, calculateFare is the name, and inside the brackets are the parameters with their types. The body is the code inside the braces.

Parts of a method header: In full, a header can have an access modifier (public, private and so on), optional keywords like static or final, the return type, the method name and the parameter list. For example: public static int max(int a, int b). If the method returns nothing, its return type is void. The method signature, which Java uses to tell methods apart, is only the name plus the parameter types, so max(int, int). The return type is not part of the signature.

Return values: A method with a non-void return type must return a value of that type on every path. int square(int x) { return x * x; } returns 25 for square(5). The return statement ends the method immediately, even inside a loop. A void method can use plain return; to exit early, for example if a withdraw amount is invalid. If a method promises an int but some if branch forgets to return, the compiler gives an error "missing return statement".

Parameters and arguments: The variables in the header are called parameters (or formal parameters). The actual values you pass in a call are called arguments (or actual parameters). In square(5), x is the parameter and 5 is the argument. Arguments must match the parameters in number, order and type, although Java will widen automatically, so you can pass an int where a double parameter is expected.

Instance methods and the calling object: In OOP most methods are instance methods: they belong to objects. When you call acc.deposit(500), the method runs with two inputs: the argument 500, and the object acc itself, which the method can reach through its fields. That is why deposit needs only one parameter even though it changes a balance. The balance comes from the object.

Local variables and scope: A variable declared inside a method, including its parameters, is a local variable. It lives on the stack only while the method runs and disappears when the method returns. Its scope is the block in which it is declared: a variable declared inside a for loop cannot be used after the loop. Fields, in contrast, live as long as the object lives. If a local variable has the same name as a field, the local one hides the field inside that method; lesson 6 shows how this.name solves that.

Java is always pass-by-value: This is a famous exam topic. When you call a method, Java copies the value of each argument into the parameter. For primitives, the number itself is copied. void addTen(int x) { x = x + 10; } then int a = 5; addTen(a); leaves a as 5, because only the copy x changed.

Passing object references: For objects, the value that is copied is the reference, the address. So the method gets a second card with the same house address. void giveBonus(Student s) { s.cgpa = s.cgpa + 0.1; } really changes the student, because both the caller's variable and s point to the same object. But if the method does s = new Student(); it only changes its own copy of the address; the caller's variable still points to the original student. People sometimes call this "pass reference by value". Java does not have pass-by-reference like C++'s int& parameters.

A trace to make it stick: Suppose main has Student r = new Student(); r.cgpa = 3.0; and calls change(r). Inside, void change(Student s) { s.cgpa = 3.5; s = new Student(); s.cgpa = 2.0; }. Step 1: s points to r's object, so its cgpa becomes 3.5. Step 2: s now points to a brand new object. Step 3: that new object's cgpa becomes 2.0. Back in main, r still points to the original object, whose cgpa is 3.5. The output of printing r.cgpa is 3.5.

Method overloading: Java lets a class have several methods with the same name, as long as their parameter lists differ in number, type or order of types. This is called method overloading. int add(int a, int b), double add(double a, double b) and int add(int a, int b, int c) can all live in one class. When you call add(2, 3), Java picks the first; add(2.5, 1.5) picks the second; add(1, 2, 3) picks the third.

Why overloading is useful: It lets you give one natural name to one idea that works on different inputs. System.out.println is the most famous example: there are versions for int, double, char, boolean, String, Object and more, so you can print anything with the same name. Without overloading you would need printInt, printDouble and so on. Overloading is a form of compile-time polymorphism, which lesson 12 discusses.

Overloading rules and traps: The return type alone cannot distinguish overloads. int area(int s) and double area(int s) together give a compile error, because a call area(5) would be ambiguous. Parameter names also do not matter; only their types and order. If no exact match exists, Java tries widening, so add(2, 3L) with only int and double versions would choose the double version, because long can widen to double but not to int.

Varargs: Sometimes you do not know how many arguments will come. Java offers variable-length arguments, written with three dots: int sum(int... nums). Inside, nums behaves like an int array. You can call sum(), sum(4), or sum(4, 6, 1, 2) and the method loops over nums. A varargs parameter must be the last parameter, and a method can have only one.

Calling one method from another: Methods of the same class can call each other directly. In an Account class, transfer(Account to, double amount) can first call this.withdraw(amount) and then to.deposit(amount). Splitting work into small methods, each with a clear name, is a core skill: each method should do one thing well and be short enough to read at a glance.

Recursion, briefly: A method can call itself; this is recursion. int fact(int n) { if (n <= 1) return 1; return n * fact(n - 1); } computes 5! as 120. Every recursive method needs a base case that stops the calls, or the stack fills up and you get a StackOverflowError. Recursion is covered deeply in Data Structures and Algorithms courses, so here just know that Java supports it.

Getting data back: A method can return only one value. If you need several, return an object that holds them, for example a Result object with gpa and grade fields, or an array. This is one of many places where small classes make life easier.

Good method design: Use a verb or verb phrase for the name: calculateGPA, sendMessage, isValid. Methods that answer yes or no often start with is or has and return boolean. Keep the number of parameters small; if you need six, maybe they belong together in a class. Avoid surprising side effects: a method called getTotal should not secretly change data.

The call stack in action: Each time a method is called, Java pushes a new frame on the stack holding that call's parameters and local variables, plus where to return. Say main calls checkout(), which calls total(), which calls applyDiscount(). The stack now has four frames, with applyDiscount on top. When applyDiscount returns 202.5, its frame is popped and total continues exactly where it left off. This is why local variables of different calls never mix, and why an exception's stack trace lists the chain of calls that led to the error, from the most recent call at the top.

Choosing overloads with null and literals: Overload resolution happens at compile time, using the declared types of the arguments. A literal 5 is an int and 5.0 is a double, so f(5) and f(5.0) can pick different versions. If you overload print(String s) and print(Object o) and call print(null), Java picks the String version, because it chooses the most specific type that matches. If two versions are equally specific, for example print(String) and print(Integer) with print(null), the compiler reports an ambiguous call and you must cast, such as print((String) null).

Real life example 1, a mobile recharge app: A Recharge class could overload a method: recharge(String number, int amount) for a normal top-up, and recharge(String number, int amount, String offerCode) for a package offer. The app's screen calls the one that matches what the user typed. Inside, both versions can call a private helper validateNumber(number) that returns a boolean, so the checking rule is written once.

Real life example 2, a shop billing system: In a grocery shop app, a method double total(double... prices) adds any number of item prices. total(120, 45, 60) gives 225. Another method double applyDiscount(double amount, double percent) returns the price after discount: applyDiscount(225, 10) returns 202.5. The bill is calculated by combining small methods, each easy to test on its own.

Common mistakes: Thinking a method can change a caller's int variable. Thinking assigning a new object to a parameter changes the caller's reference. Trying to overload by return type only. Forgetting return on some path. Using a local variable outside its block. Confusing parameters with arguments in definitions.

What exams ask: "What is method overloading? Give an example", "Is Java pass-by-value or pass-by-reference? Explain with code", "Differentiate between parameters and arguments", "Can we overload a method by changing only its return type?" (answer: no), and output tracing questions with objects passed to methods.

Recap: A method has a return type, a name and parameters; its signature is the name plus parameter types. Java always passes copies: copies of numbers for primitives and copies of references for objects, so methods can change an object's contents but not the caller's variable. Overloading gives one name many parameter lists and is resolved at compile time. Next, we meet a special kind of method that runs when an object is born: the constructor.
key_points: A method has a return type, name and parameter list; the signature is name plus parameter types.
Parameters are in the definition; arguments are the values passed in a call.
Java is always pass-by-value: primitives are copied, object references are copied.
A method can change an object's fields through a copied reference, but not the caller's variable.
Overloading: same name, different parameter lists; return type alone is not enough.
Varargs (int... nums) accepts any number of arguments and must come last.
Local variables live only during the call and only inside their block.
lessons.tip: Whenever you see an object passed to a method, draw two arrows to the same object box. Then check whether the method changes the object or only its own arrow.
