quiz.q: Which is part of a Java method signature?
quiz.explain: Java tells methods apart by name and the types/order of parameters.

quiz.q: int a = 5; addTen(a); where addTen sets its parameter x = x + 10. What is a now?
quiz.explain: Only the copy x changed; Java passes primitives by value.

quiz.q: Which pair is NOT a valid overload?
options: int f(int x) and double f(int y)
int f(int x) and int f(double x)
int f(int x) and int f(int x, int y)
int f(int x, double y) and int f(double x, int y)
quiz.explain: Differing only in return type (and parameter name) is a compile error.

quiz.q: A method receives a Student reference s and runs s.cgpa = 3.5. What happens to the caller's object?
quiz.explain: The copied reference still points to the same object.

quiz.q: Where must a varargs parameter appear?
quiz.explain: A varargs parameter must be the last one, and there can be only one.

lessons.title: Constructors and Object Lifetime
lessons.content:
When a baby is born in a hospital in Bangladesh, a few things happen right away: the baby gets a name, a birth time is written down, and a birth registration form is filled in. Nobody waits until the child is ten to decide its name. Objects are similar. The moment an object is created, it should be set up with sensible starting values. In Java, the special code that does this setup is called a constructor. This lesson covers constructors and the whole life of an object, from birth to garbage collection.

The problem without constructors: In lesson 3 we wrote Student s = new Student(); s.name = "Rahim"; s.roll = 101;. That works, but it is risky. Someone might forget to set the roll, leaving it 0, or set name but not cgpa. The object exists for a while in a half-ready state. With many fields and many objects, these gaps cause bugs. We want the object to be complete from the very first moment.

What a constructor is: A constructor is a special block of code in a class that runs automatically when you create an object with new. It has two special features: its name is exactly the same as the class name, and it has no return type, not even void. class Student { String name; int roll; Student(String n, int r) { name = n; roll = r; } } Now new Student("Rahim", 101) creates the object and immediately fills in name and roll.

How new and the constructor work together: When Java runs new Student("Rahim", 101), it does roughly four things in order. It allocates memory on the heap for a Student object. It sets every field to its default value (null, 0, false). It runs any field initializers and then the constructor body with the given arguments. Finally new returns the reference to the finished object, which is stored in your variable. So the constructor does not create the object; new does. The constructor initializes it.

The default constructor: If you write a class with no constructor at all, the Java compiler quietly adds one for you: a public, no-argument constructor with an empty body (it just calls the parent's no-argument constructor, which matters in lesson 10). That is why new Student() worked in lesson 3. This compiler-added one is called the default constructor.

The trap with default constructors: As soon as you write any constructor yourself, the compiler stops adding the default one. So if Student has only Student(String n, int r), then new Student() no longer compiles: "constructor Student in class Student cannot be applied to given types". If you still want a no-argument option, write it yourself. This catches many students in lab exams.

No-argument versus parameterized constructors: A constructor with no parameters is a no-arg constructor; you write one when you want a sensible default object, like Student() { name = "Unknown"; roll = -1; }. A constructor with parameters is a parameterized constructor; it lets the caller choose the starting values. Most real classes have at least one parameterized constructor, because objects usually need some data to be meaningful.

Constructor overloading: Just like methods, constructors can be overloaded, as long as their parameter lists differ. class Rectangle { double w, h; Rectangle() { w = 1; h = 1; } Rectangle(double side) { w = side; h = side; } Rectangle(double w0, double h0) { w = w0; h = h0; } } Now new Rectangle() makes a 1 by 1 square, new Rectangle(5) makes a 5 by 5 square, and new Rectangle(4, 3) makes a 4 by 3 rectangle. The caller picks whichever is most convenient.

Constructor chaining with this(...): Look at the Rectangle above: the logic of setting w and h is repeated three times. Java lets one constructor call another constructor of the same class using this(...). Rewrite as Rectangle() { this(1, 1); } Rectangle(double side) { this(side, side); } Rectangle(double w0, double h0) { w = w0; h = h0; }. Now all the real work lives in one place. The rule: this(...) must be the very first statement in the constructor, and a constructor cannot call itself in a loop of this() calls.

Validation in constructors: A constructor is the best place to reject bad data, because it guards the entrance. Account(String owner, double opening) { if (opening < 500) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Minimum opening balance is 500"); this.owner = owner; balance = opening; }. If the rule fails, the object is never created. Exceptions are covered in lesson 17; for now, notice that a constructor can refuse to build a broken object.

Copy constructors: Java has no automatic copy constructor like C++, but you can write one: a constructor that takes another object of the same class and copies its fields. Student(Student other) { name = other.name; roll = other.roll; cgpa = other.cgpa; }. Then Student copy = new Student(original); makes a separate object with the same values. Changing copy.cgpa no longer affects original, unlike Student copy = original;, which only copies the reference.

Field initializers: You can give a field a starting value where you declare it: int attempts = 3; or String country = "Bangladesh";. These run for every object before the constructor body. They are handy for values that are the same for all new objects. If the constructor also sets the field, the constructor's value wins, because it runs later.

Instance initializer blocks: A block of code in braces directly inside the class, not in any method, is an instance initializer block. { System.out.println("An object is being created"); } It runs every time an object is created, before the constructor body, in the order it appears with field initializers. They are rarely used in everyday code, but exam questions like to ask about the order of execution.

Order of initialization, step by step: For new Student("Rahim", 101): first all fields get default values; then field initializers and instance initializer blocks run, from top to bottom; then the constructor body runs. If there is a parent class, the parent part is initialized first (lesson 10). Static parts, which run once when the class is first loaded, come before all of this (lesson 6). A tracing question that prints messages from each part is a classic exam item.

A worked order-of-execution trace: Consider class Demo { int x = 5; { System.out.println("block x=" + x); x = 10; } Demo() { System.out.println("ctor x=" + x); x = 20; } }. When main runs Demo d = new Demo(); System.out.println("main x=" + d.x);, the steps are: x starts at default 0, then the field initializer sets it to 5, then the instance block prints "block x=5" and sets x to 10, then the constructor prints "ctor x=10" and sets x to 20, and finally main prints "main x=20". Practise writing out these lines by hand; examiners love this exact shape of question.

Can constructors be private? Yes. A private constructor stops other classes from creating objects with new. This is used in utility classes that only have static methods, like Java's own Math class, and in the Singleton design pattern, where a class allows exactly one object (lesson 25).

What constructors cannot do: They cannot have a return type; if you write void Student() it becomes an ordinary method named Student, and it will not run on new, which is a sneaky bug. They are not inherited by subclasses. They cannot be called like a normal method, as in s.Student(). And they cannot be abstract, static or final.

Object lifetime: An object is born with new and its constructor. It lives as long as at least one reference can reach it, directly or through other objects. When no reference can reach it, it becomes eligible for garbage collection. Common ways this happens: a local variable goes out of scope when its method returns, a reference is set to null, or the reference is pointed at another object.

Garbage collection: Java's garbage collector (GC) is part of the JVM. It periodically finds unreachable objects and reclaims their memory. You cannot control exactly when it runs; System.gc() is only a polite request, not a command. The benefit is huge: no forgotten free() calls, no double frees, no dangling pointers. The cost is that you do not control timing, and memory can still leak if you keep references you no longer need, such as an ever-growing list.

finalize and destructors: C++ has destructors, special functions that run when an object is destroyed, used to release resources (lesson 22). Java had a similar method called finalize(), but it was unreliable because you never know when, or even whether, it runs, and it has been deprecated since Java 9. In modern Java, to release resources like files or network connections, you use try-with-resources and close(), shown in lessons 17 and 20.

Real life example 1, a bKash style account: class MobileAccount { String number; String pin; double balance; MobileAccount(String number, String pin) { this.number = number; this.pin = pin; balance = 0; } }. Every new account must have a phone number and a PIN from the start; there is no such thing as an account without a number. A second constructor MobileAccount(String number, String pin, double bonus) can call this(number, pin) and then add a sign-up bonus.

Real life example 2, Pathao ride requests: class Ride { String pickup, drop; double km; String status; Ride(String pickup, String drop, double km) { this.pickup = pickup; this.drop = drop; this.km = km; status = "REQUESTED"; } }. Every ride starts in the REQUESTED state, so the constructor sets it. Later methods like accept() and complete() change the status. When the ride is finished and removed from the app's active list, no reference points to it, and the GC can clean it up.

Common mistakes: Writing a return type on a constructor. Expecting a default constructor after writing a parameterized one. Putting this(...) on the second line. Thinking the constructor creates the object (new does). Thinking finalize() is a reliable destructor. Thinking Student b = a; calls a copy constructor.

What exams ask: "What is a constructor? How is it different from a method?" (same name as class, no return type, called automatically, not inherited), "What is a default constructor?", "Explain constructor overloading and constructor chaining with an example", "Can a constructor be private? Why?", and "Show the order of execution" tracing questions with initializer blocks.

Recap: Constructors initialize new objects; they share the class name and have no return type. Java supplies a default constructor only when you write none. Constructors can be overloaded and chained with this(...), which must be the first statement. Field initializers and instance blocks run before the constructor body. Objects live while reachable, and the garbage collector frees them later. Next we meet three keywords that shape how classes and objects share data: this, static and final.
key_points: A constructor has the class name and no return type; it runs automatically on new.
new allocates the object; the constructor initializes it.
Java adds a default no-arg constructor only if you write no constructor.
Constructors can be overloaded and chained with this(...), which must be the first statement.
A copy constructor creates a separate object with the same field values.
Order: default values, then field initializers and instance blocks, then the constructor body.
Objects live while reachable; the garbage collector frees them at a time you do not control.
finalize() is deprecated; release resources with close() and try-with-resources.
lessons.tip: When you meet a new class, first ask: what must every object have from the start? Those fields go into the constructor's parameters.
lessons.task: Write a Rectangle class with three constructors (none, one side, width and height) chained with this(...). Print the area of one object made with each constructor.

quiz.q: Which is true about a Java constructor?
options: It has the same name as the class and no return type
It can be called like s.Student()
quiz.explain: Constructors share the class name and have no return type at all.

quiz.q: A class has only Student(String n). What does new Student() do?
quiz.explain: Once you write any constructor, the compiler no longer adds the default one.

quiz.q: Where must this(...) appear inside a constructor?
quiz.explain: A this(...) call must be the first statement of the constructor.

quiz.q: Which runs first when an object is created?
quiz.explain: Memory is set to default values before any initializer or constructor code runs.

quiz.q: Why is a constructor sometimes made private?
options: To stop other classes from creating objects with new, e.g. Singleton
quiz.explain: Private constructors are used in utility classes and the Singleton pattern.

lessons.title: this, static and final
lessons.content:
Imagine a school hostel. Every student has their own bed, own trunk and own toothbrush. But there is only one water tank on the roof, one notice board and one hostel superintendent, shared by everyone. If one student writes on the notice board, everyone sees it. Some things belong to each person; some things belong to the whole hostel. Java classes have exactly the same split, and the keyword static is how you say "this belongs to the whole class, not to one object". In this lesson we study three small but powerful keywords: this, static and final.

Part 1, the keyword this: Inside an instance method or constructor, this is a reference to the current object, the object on which the method was called. When you call rahim.introduce(), inside introduce this refers to rahim. When you call fatima.introduce(), this refers to fatima. You can think of it as the object pointing at itself and saying "me".

Use 1, resolving name clashes: The most common use of this is in constructors and setters where a parameter has the same name as a field. class Student { String name; Student(String name) { name = name; } } looks right but does nothing useful: inside the constructor, name means the parameter, so you assign the parameter to itself and the field stays null. The fix is this.name = name;. Now this.name means the field of the current object and name means the parameter. This pattern is so common that most Java code uses it.

Use 2, calling another constructor: As lesson 5 showed, this(...) as the first statement of a constructor calls another constructor of the same class. Rectangle(double side) { this(side, side); }. Note the difference: this.something refers to a member, while this(...) with brackets right after it calls a constructor.

Use 3, passing the current object: Sometimes an object needs to hand itself to another object. In a game, a Player might register with a Team: team.addPlayer(this);. Or a Student could enroll in a Course: course.enroll(this);. Here this is passed like any other reference.

Use 4, returning the current object: A method can return this so calls can be chained, a style called a fluent interface. class Order { int items; Order add(int n) { items += n; return this; } } lets you write order.add(2).add(3).add(1); and items ends up 6. Java's StringBuilder works this way, which you will see in lesson 8.

Where this cannot be used: this only exists when there is a current object. Inside a static method there is no current object, so using this or any instance field directly there is a compile error. This leads us to static.

Part 2, static fields: A field marked static belongs to the class itself, not to any object. There is exactly one copy, shared by every object of the class, and it exists even if no object has been created. class Student { String name; static String university = "Dhaka University"; }. All Student objects share the same university. Change it once, and every student sees the change.

Instance versus static, side by side: An instance variable (non-static field) has one copy per object; 60 students means 60 names. A static variable has one copy per class; 60 students still means one university field. Instance variables are created when an object is created and live on the heap inside the object. Static variables are created when the class is loaded and live in a special area for class data. The usual way to access a static field is through the class name: Student.university, not rahim.university, although the second form also compiles.

A classic example, counting objects: class Student { static int count = 0; int id; Student() { count++; id = count; } }. Create three students: new Student(), new Student(), new Student(). After that, Student.count is 3, and the objects have ids 1, 2 and 3. If count were not static, each object would have its own count, which would always be 1, and the counting would fail. This "object counter" is one of the most common exam programs.

Static methods: A static method belongs to the class and is called with the class name: Math.sqrt(16), Integer.parseInt("42"). It does not need an object, so it has no this. Inside a static method you can use static fields and other static methods directly, but you cannot use instance fields or instance methods directly, because there is no particular object to take them from. If you need an instance member, you must create or receive an object: Student s = new Student(); s.introduce();.

Why main is static: When you run java Hello, no object of Hello exists yet. The JVM must call main without creating an object, so main is declared static. That is also why beginners get the error "non-static method cannot be referenced from a static context" when they call an instance method directly from main. The fix is to make an object first, or to make the helper method static if it really does not need object data.

When to make something static: Ask "does this depend on a particular object?" A method that converts taka to dollars at a given rate does not depend on any object, so static is fine: static double toDollar(double taka, double rate). A method that withdraws money from an account depends on that account's balance, so it must be an instance method. Constants and shared counters are good static fields. Overusing static turns your code back into procedural code with global variables, so use it with care.

Static blocks: A static block, written static { ... } inside a class, runs once when the class is loaded, before any object is created and before main if it is in the main class. It is used to initialize complex static data, for example filling a static table of district codes. Order matters: static blocks and static field initializers run first, once, top to bottom; instance initializers and constructors run every time an object is made.

Part 3, the keyword final: final means "cannot be changed after it is set". It can be applied to variables, methods and classes, with a different effect each time.

final variables: A final local variable or field can be assigned only once. final int MAX_SEATS = 40; makes a constant. A final instance field must be assigned exactly once, either where it is declared or in every constructor; this is called a blank final field when it is set in the constructor, as in class Student { final int roll; Student(int roll) { this.roll = roll; } }. After that, roll can never change, which suits an ID.

static final constants: Combine both keywords for class-wide constants: static final double VAT = 0.15; or public static final int MAX_MARKS = 100;. There is one copy and it never changes. By convention their names are in UPPER_SNAKE_CASE. Math.PI is exactly this kind of constant.

final references are not frozen objects: This is a famous trap. final Student s = new Student("Rahim"); means the variable s can never point to a different object, so s = new Student("Karim"); does not compile. But s.name = "Rahim Uddin"; is allowed, because you are changing the object, not the reference. final protects the arrow, not the box. To make the object itself unchangeable you need an immutable class, covered in lesson 7.

final methods and final classes, a preview: A final method cannot be overridden by a subclass, and a final class cannot be extended at all. String is a final class in Java. These matter once we learn inheritance, so lesson 11 explains them properly.

A tracing example with static and instance together: class Counter { static int s = 0; int i = 0; void tick() { s++; i++; } }. Make Counter a = new Counter(); Counter b = new Counter(); then call a.tick(); a.tick(); b.tick();. Object a's i is 2 and object b's i is 1, because each has its own i. But s is 3, because all three calls increased the one shared s. Printing a.s and b.s both show 3, which is why accessing static fields through an object name is legal but misleading; Counter.s says the truth clearly.

Static and memory: Because a static field lives as long as its class is loaded, which in a normal program means until the program ends, anything a static field refers to also stays alive. A static List that keeps growing is a classic way to leak memory in Java, because the garbage collector can never free objects that a static field can still reach. Another warning: static fields are shared by every part of the program, so in multithreaded code (lesson 21) two threads changing the same static counter at once can corrupt it unless the access is synchronized.

Static imports, a small extra: If you use Math constants and methods a lot, you can write import static java.lang.Math.*; at the top of the file and then just write sqrt(16) or PI instead of Math.sqrt(16) and Math.PI. Use this lightly, because when many static imports are mixed, readers cannot tell which class a name came from.

Real life example 1, a cinema hall booking system: class Ticket { static int sold = 0; static final int CAPACITY = 300; final int seatNo; String buyer; Ticket(String buyer) { if (sold >= CAPACITY) throw new IllegalStateException("House full"); sold++; seatNo = sold; this.buyer = buyer; } }. sold is shared and counts all tickets. CAPACITY is a constant. seatNo is final, so a ticket's seat cannot change after printing. this.buyer = buyer resolves the name clash.

Real life example 2, a utility class for Bangladesh phone numbers: class PhoneUtil { private PhoneUtil() {} static boolean isValidBD(String n) { return n.length() == 11 && n.startsWith("01"); } }. Nobody needs a PhoneUtil object, so the constructor is private and the method is static: PhoneUtil.isValidBD("01712345678") returns true. This is the same pattern as Java's Math class.

Common mistakes: Writing name = name in a constructor. Using this inside a static method. Calling an instance method directly from main. Making everything static to silence compiler errors. Thinking a final reference makes the object unchangeable. Forgetting to assign a final field in one of the constructors, which is a compile error.

What exams ask: "What are the uses of the this keyword?", "Differentiate between static and instance variables", "Why is main declared static?", "Write a program to count the number of objects created", "Can a static method access instance variables? Why not?", and "Explain the final keyword with variables, methods and classes".

Recap: this refers to the current object and is used to resolve name clashes, chain constructors, pass or return the current object. static members belong to the class: one shared copy, accessed by class name, with no this inside static methods. static blocks run once at class loading. final makes a variable assign-once, a method non-overridable and a class non-extendable, and final references still allow the object to change. Next, encapsulation shows how to protect an object's data with access modifiers.
key_points: this is a reference to the current object; it does not exist in static methods.
this.name = name resolves a clash between a field and a parameter.
this(...) calls another constructor; this can also be passed or returned for chaining.
A static field has one copy shared by all objects and exists before any object.
Static methods are called by class name and cannot use instance members directly.
main is static so the JVM can call it without creating an object.
static blocks run once when the class loads, before objects and main.
final variables are assign-once; a final reference cannot be re-pointed but its object can still change.
lessons.tip: Before typing static, ask: does this need a particular object? If yes, it is an instance member. If no, static may be fine.
lessons.task: Write a Student class with a static counter that gives each new object an id (1, 2, 3...). Create 4 students and print each id plus Student.count.

quiz.q: Inside rahim.introduce(), what does this refer to?
quiz.explain: this refers to the object on which the method was called.

quiz.q: What is wrong with Student(String name) { name = name; }?
options: The field is never set; it assigns the parameter to itself
quiz.explain: Use this.name = name to assign the field.

quiz.q: How many copies of a static field exist if 50 objects are created?
quiz.explain: A static field belongs to the class and has a single shared copy.

quiz.q: Why can a static method not use instance fields directly?
options: There is no current object (no this)
quiz.explain: Static methods run without any object, so there is no instance data to use.

quiz.q: final Student s = new Student(); Which line compiles?
quiz.explain: final stops re-pointing the reference, but the object's fields can still change.

lessons.title: Encapsulation and Access Modifiers
lessons.content:
Think about an ATM booth of your bank. Inside the machine there is a big box full of cash. You cannot open the box and take out notes with your hands. Instead there is a small set of buttons: check balance, withdraw, change PIN. Each button checks rules first: is your PIN correct, do you have enough money, is the amount a multiple of 500? The cash is hidden; the buttons are the only way in. That is encapsulation, the first pillar of OOP, and the subject of this lesson.

What encapsulation means: Encapsulation is the bundling of data and the methods that work on that data into a single unit, the class, together with restricting direct access to the data from outside. Two ideas are joined here. Bundling: the balance and the deposit and withdraw methods live together in Account. Hiding: other code cannot touch balance directly; it must go through the methods. The hiding part is often called data hiding or information hiding.

Why we need it, a broken example: class Account { double balance; }. Any code anywhere can write acc.balance = -50000; or acc.balance = acc.balance * 100;. No rule stops it. In a real bank system written by fifty programmers, sooner or later someone will do something silly, and the account will be in an impossible state. We want the class itself to be the guard of its own data.

Access modifiers: Java controls who can see a member using four access levels. private: visible only inside the same class. default, also called package-private, when you write no modifier at all: visible inside the same package. protected: visible inside the same package and in subclasses, even in other packages. public: visible everywhere. From most restrictive to least: private, default, protected, public.

The access table: Think of four places code might be: the same class, another class in the same package, a subclass in a different package, and an unrelated class in a different package. private allows only the first. default allows the first two. protected allows the first three. public allows all four. Draw this as a 4 by 4 table of yes and no; it is one of the most asked diagrams in exams. Lesson 16 explains packages more, and lesson 10 explains subclasses.

Access for classes: A top-level class can only be public or default. A public class is usable from any package and must live in a file with the same name. A default class is usable only within its package, which is handy for helper classes that outsiders should not see. Nested classes, written inside another class, can also be private or protected.

The encapsulated Account: class Account { private String owner; private double balance; public Account(String owner, double opening) { this.owner = owner; if (opening < 0) opening = 0; balance = opening; } public double getBalance() { return balance; } public void deposit(double amt) { if (amt <= 0) return; balance += amt; } public boolean withdraw(double amt) { if (amt <= 0 || amt > balance) return false; balance -= amt; return true; } }. Now acc.balance = -50000; does not compile, because balance is private. The only ways in are the public methods, and each one checks its rules.

Getters and setters: A getter (accessor) is a public method that returns the value of a private field, named getX by convention, or isX for booleans: getBalance(), isActive(). A setter (mutator) is a public method that changes a private field, named setX: setPhone(String p). They look like extra typing, but they give the class a chance to check, convert or log values, and to change how data is stored later without breaking other code.

Validation in setters: class Student { private double cgpa; public void setCgpa(double c) { if (c < 0.0 || c > 4.0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("CGPA must be 0 to 4"); cgpa = c; } }. Now no part of the program can ever store a CGPA of 5.7. One rule, in one place, protects every student object. Without encapsulation you would have to repeat that check everywhere a CGPA is set, and someone would forget.

Not every field needs a setter: Beginners often generate a getter and setter for every field, which makes private almost meaningless. Ask what outsiders really need. A bank balance should have a getter but no setter, only deposit and withdraw. A roll number set in the constructor may need no setter at all. A password field should have no getter. Exposing only what is needed is the spirit of encapsulation.

Hiding the representation: Encapsulation also lets you change how data is stored inside without affecting users of the class. Suppose Account first stores balance as a double in taka. Later the bank decides to store paisa as a long to avoid rounding errors: private long paisa;. If getBalance() still returns paisa / 100.0, no other class needs to change. Code that used acc.balance directly would all break. This freedom to change the inside is one of the biggest practical benefits.

Read-only and write-only properties: A field with only a getter is read-only from outside, like an account number. A field with only a setter is write-only, like a PIN that can be changed but never read back. Combining private fields with a chosen set of methods lets you design exactly what is allowed.

Encapsulation versus abstraction: These two are often confused. Encapsulation is about how: putting data and code together and controlling access with modifiers, so the inside cannot be misused. Abstraction is about what: exposing a simple idea and hiding complexity, so users think only about essentials. An ATM's buttons are abstraction (you just think "withdraw"); the locked cash box behind them is encapsulation. In code, private fields are an encapsulation tool, while interfaces and abstract classes are abstraction tools (lessons 13 and 14).

Immutable classes: An immutable object cannot change after it is created. Java's String is immutable. To make your own immutable class: make the class final so nobody can subclass it and add changing methods; make all fields private and final; set them only in the constructor; provide getters but no setters; and if a field refers to a mutable object, such as an array, copy it in the constructor and return copies from getters. final class Point { private final int x, y; Point(int x, int y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; } int getX() { return x; } int getY() { return y; } }.

Why immutability helps: An immutable object can be shared freely between parts of a program, or between threads (lesson 21), with no fear that someone will change it behind your back. It is always in a valid state, because the constructor checked it once. To "change" it, you create a new object: p.moveRight() returns new Point(x + 1, y). Values like dates, money amounts and coordinates are often made immutable.

The leaking reference trap: Suppose class Team { private String[] players; public String[] getPlayers() { return players; } }. The field is private, but the getter returns the actual array reference. Outside code can do team.getPlayers()[0] = "Hacker"; and change the team. Encapsulation has leaked. The fix is to return a copy: return players.clone();, or an unmodifiable list in modern code. The same applies when a constructor receives a mutable object: store a copy, not the caller's reference.

Benefits of encapsulation, summarized: Data integrity, because rules are enforced in one place. Flexibility, because the internal representation can change. Easier debugging, because if a field goes wrong only the class's own methods could have done it. Clear interfaces, because the public methods document what the class offers. Security, because sensitive data like PINs is not exposed.

Private helper methods: Fields are not the only things to hide. Methods that are just internal steps should be private too. In an Account class, a method private boolean isValidAmount(double a) { return a > 0 && a <= 50000; } can be used by deposit, withdraw and transfer, but outsiders have no reason to call it. Keeping helpers private means you can rename, split or delete them later without breaking anyone, because nobody outside could depend on them.

A tiny design exercise: Design a Thermometer class for a fridge. The temperature must stay between -20 and 10 degrees. Field: private double temp. Constructor: takes a starting temperature and rejects values outside the range. Getter: getTemp(). No plain setter; instead, methods colder() and warmer() change temp by 1 degree, but refuse to go past the limits. Notice how thinking about the rules first decides which methods exist. This is exactly the kind of short design answer that earns full marks.

Encapsulation in other languages: C++ uses the same words, private, protected and public, but writes them as sections: class Account { private: double balance; public: void deposit(double a); };, and members of a C++ class are private by default (lesson 22). Python has no enforced private; it uses a naming convention, a leading underscore like _balance, to say "please do not touch". The idea is the same everywhere, but Java and C++ let the compiler enforce it.

Real life example 1, a bKash wallet: class Wallet { private String pin; private double balance; public boolean sendMoney(Wallet to, double amt, String enteredPin) { if (!pin.equals(enteredPin) || amt <= 0 || amt > balance) return false; balance -= amt; to.receive(amt); return true; } private void receive(double amt) { balance += amt; } }. Note that receive is private: only Wallet objects themselves can call it, so outsiders cannot create money. In Java, private means private to the class, so one Wallet object can call another Wallet object's private method.

Real life example 2, a student result portal: class Result { private int[] marks; public Result(int[] marks) { for (int m : marks) if (m < 0 || m > 100) throw new IllegalArgumentException("bad mark"); this.marks = marks.clone(); } public double average() { int sum = 0; for (int m : marks) sum += m; return (double) sum / marks.length; } }. Marks are checked once, copied so nobody can change them from outside, and there is no setter. Teachers can see the average; nobody can quietly bump a mark from 38 to 80.

Common mistakes: Making fields public "to keep it simple". Writing a setter for everything. Returning internal arrays or lists directly. Confusing default (no modifier) with public. Thinking protected means "only subclasses" (it also includes the same package). Thinking private hides data from other objects of the same class (it does not; privacy is per class).

What exams ask: "Define encapsulation with an example", "What are access modifiers? Show their visibility in a table", "Why should fields be private?", "Write a BankAccount class with proper encapsulation", "Differentiate between encapsulation and abstraction", and "How do you make a class immutable?".

Recap: Encapsulation bundles data and methods and hides the data behind access modifiers. private, default, protected and public give increasing visibility. Getters and setters, used thoughtfully, guard and validate data, and let the internal representation change freely. Immutable classes take this further: final fields, no setters, defensive copies. Next, we look at the most used class in Java, String, and the wrapper classes, both of which are built on these ideas.
key_points: Encapsulation = bundling data with its methods + hiding the data from direct outside access.
Access levels from strict to open: private, default (package), protected, public.
protected allows the same package and subclasses in other packages.
Getters and setters let the class validate, convert and protect its data.
Only expose what is needed: not every field needs a setter (or a getter).
Encapsulation lets the internal representation change without breaking other classes.
Immutable class: final class, private final fields, no setters, defensive copies.
Returning an internal array or list directly leaks encapsulation.
lessons.tip: For every field ask two questions: should outsiders read it, and should outsiders change it? Your answers decide which getters and setters exist.
