quiz.explain: Images are binary data; character streams would corrupt them.

quiz.q: What does BufferedReader.readLine() return at the end of the file?
quiz.explain: null signals that there are no more lines.

quiz.q: How do you open log.txt to add lines at the end?
quiz.explain: The true argument turns on append mode.

quiz.q: A field marked transient is:
quiz.explain: After deserialization it has its default value.

quiz.q: Wrapping a FileReader inside a BufferedReader is an example of which pattern?
quiz.explain: Each wrapper adds behaviour to the stream it wraps.

lessons.title: Multithreading
lessons.content:
Watch a busy restaurant kitchen in Old Dhaka during iftar time. One cook fries piyaju, another stirs haleem, a third packs orders, and the manager takes phone calls. They all work at the same time in the same kitchen, sharing the same stove and the same counter. Things go fast because work happens in parallel, but there is a risk: two cooks reaching for the same pan at the same moment can cause a mess. A Java program can work like this kitchen, running several tasks at once, using threads. This lesson introduces multithreading and the problems of sharing.

Process versus thread: A process is a running program with its own memory space; your browser and your music player are different processes, and one cannot directly read the other's memory. A thread is a smaller unit of execution inside a process. All threads of a process share its heap memory, its objects and its open files, but each thread has its own stack and its own position in the code. Creating and switching threads is cheaper than processes, and sharing memory makes communication easy, which is also what makes it dangerous.

Why use threads: Responsiveness, because a long task like downloading a file can run in the background while the user interface stays usable. Speed, because modern phones and laptops have several CPU cores, and separate threads can run truly in parallel on them. And natural modelling, because many real systems, such as a server handling hundreds of users or a game with music, animation and input, really are many activities happening at once.

The main thread: Every Java program starts with one thread, the main thread, which runs main. When you create more threads, they run alongside it. The program ends when all non-daemon threads have finished, not necessarily when main returns.

Creating a thread by extending Thread: class Downloader extends Thread { private final String file; Downloader(String file) { this.file = file; } @Override public void run() { System.out.println("Downloading " + file); } }. Then new Downloader("song.mp3").start();. The run method holds the work. Calling start() asks the JVM to create a new thread of execution that will call run.

start versus run, the classic mistake: If you call d.run() directly, no new thread is created; run simply executes in the current thread like any normal method, and nothing happens in parallel. Only start() creates the new thread. Also, a thread can be started only once; calling start() twice on the same Thread object throws IllegalThreadStateException.

Creating a thread with Runnable: The more flexible way is to implement the Runnable interface, which has the single method void run(), and pass it to a Thread. class PrintTask implements Runnable { public void run() { for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++) System.out.println("Task " + i); } } then Thread t = new Thread(new PrintTask()); t.start();. Since Runnable is a functional interface (lesson 14), you can also write new Thread(() -> System.out.println("Hello from a thread")).start();.

Thread versus Runnable: Extending Thread uses up your one chance at class inheritance (lesson 10), so the class cannot extend anything else. Implementing Runnable keeps your class free to extend another class, separates the task (what to do) from the worker (the thread), and lets the same task object be given to thread pools. For these reasons Runnable, or a lambda, is preferred in most code. This comparison is a frequent exam question.

Unpredictable order: Once several threads are running, the operating system's scheduler decides which runs when, switching between them very quickly. If two threads each print 1 to 3, the output might be 1 1 2 3 2 3 one time and 1 2 1 3 2 3 the next. You cannot assume any order unless you coordinate the threads. This non-determinism is the source of most threading bugs, because a bug may appear once in a thousand runs.

The thread lifecycle: A thread moves through states. New: created but start() not yet called. Runnable: started and ready to run or running; many textbooks split this into ready and running. Blocked: waiting to acquire a lock held by another thread. Waiting or timed waiting: paused by methods such as wait(), join() or sleep(ms) until something happens or time passes. Terminated (often called dead): run has finished. Java's Thread.State enum names them NEW, RUNNABLE, BLOCKED, WAITING, TIMED_WAITING and TERMINATED. Drawing these states with arrows is a standard exam answer.

sleep and join: Thread.sleep(1000) pauses the current thread for about one second and throws the checked InterruptedException, which must be caught or declared. t.join() makes the current thread wait until thread t finishes. For example, main can start three download threads and then call join on each, so it prints "All downloads complete" only after all three are done.

Priorities and daemon threads: Each thread has a priority from 1 (Thread.MIN_PRIORITY) to 10 (Thread.MAX_PRIORITY), with 5 as the normal default. Priorities are only hints to the scheduler and behave differently on different systems, so correct programs must never depend on them. A daemon thread, marked with setDaemon(true) before start, is a background helper, such as an autosave timer; the JVM does not wait for daemon threads before exiting.

Shared data and race conditions: Now the danger. class Counter { int count = 0; void increment() { count++; } }. Two threads each call increment() 10,000 times on the same Counter. You expect 20,000, but you will often get less, maybe 17,342. Why? count++ is not one step; it is read count, add one, write count. If both threads read 100 at the same moment, both write 101, and one increment is lost. A situation where the result depends on the timing of threads is called a race condition.

Critical sections and synchronized: The part of code that touches shared data and must not be run by two threads at once is called a critical section. Java protects it with the synchronized keyword: synchronized void increment() { count++; }. Every object has an internal lock, also called a monitor. A thread must acquire the object's lock before entering a synchronized method, and other threads trying to enter any synchronized method of the same object wait in the blocked state until the lock is released. Now the counter always reaches exactly 20,000.

Synchronized blocks: You can lock only part of a method, and choose the lock object: void transfer(double amt) { validate(amt); synchronized (this) { balance -= amt; } log(amt); }. Smaller critical sections let more work run in parallel. A static synchronized method locks the Class object instead of an instance, protecting static data shared by all objects.

Thread communication with wait and notify: Sometimes a thread must wait for a condition, such as a consumer waiting for a producer to put an item in a buffer. Inside a synchronized block, wait() releases the lock and pauses the thread until another thread calls notify() or notifyAll() on the same object. The waiting thread should always check its condition in a loop: while (queue.isEmpty()) wait();. These methods come from the Object class (lesson 15) and must be called while holding the object's lock, or they throw IllegalMonitorStateException.

Deadlock: A deadlock happens when threads wait for each other forever. Thread A holds lock X and waits for lock Y, while thread B holds lock Y and waits for lock X. Neither can continue, and the program freezes. Imagine two rickshaws facing each other in a narrow lane in Puran Dhaka, each waiting for the other to back out. A simple prevention rule is to always acquire multiple locks in the same global order, for example always lock the account with the smaller account number first.

Immutability helps concurrency: Remember immutable classes from lesson 7. If an object can never change after construction, any number of threads can read it at the same time with no locks and no race conditions, because there is nothing to race over. This is why String is safe to share across threads, and why many concurrent designs pass immutable messages between threads instead of sharing mutable objects. Less shared mutable state means fewer places that need synchronized.

Higher-level tools, briefly: Modern Java offers safer building blocks in java.util.concurrent. ExecutorService manages a pool of threads so you submit tasks instead of creating threads by hand: ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4); pool.submit(task); pool.shutdown();. AtomicInteger gives thread-safe counters without synchronized: counter.incrementAndGet(). ConcurrentHashMap is a thread-safe map. Your course may only mention them, but real projects use them heavily.

Threads in GUIs and apps: In desktop and mobile apps, one special thread draws the screen and handles clicks (lesson 24). If you do a slow job such as a network call on that thread, the app freezes. The rule is: do slow work on a background thread, then send the result back to the UI thread to update the screen. Android shows an "Application Not Responding" dialog when the main thread is blocked for too long.

Real life example 1, a bank account shared by two ATMs: A joint account with Tk 10,000 is used at two ATMs at once, each withdrawing Tk 8,000. Without synchronization, both threads may check balance >= 8000 before either subtracts, so both succeed and the balance becomes -6,000. Making withdraw synchronized means the second ATM's thread waits until the first finishes, then sees a balance of 2,000 and correctly refuses. This is exactly why banking software must handle concurrency carefully.

Real life example 2, a food delivery app's server: When thousands of people order at lunchtime, the server handles each request on a thread from a pool. Order details are local to each thread, which is safe. But the restaurant's available stock of kacchi biryani is shared, so reducing it must be synchronized or done with an atomic operation; otherwise two customers could both buy the last plate. Meanwhile a background daemon thread sends reminder notifications every few minutes.

Common mistakes: Calling run() instead of start(). Starting the same thread twice. Assuming threads run in a fixed order. Sharing mutable data without synchronization. Calling wait or notify outside a synchronized block. Using if instead of while around wait. Locking in different orders and creating deadlocks. Relying on thread priorities for correctness.

What exams ask: "Differentiate between a process and a thread", "What are the two ways to create a thread in Java? Which is better and why?", "Explain the life cycle of a thread with a diagram", "What is the difference between start() and run()?", "What is a race condition? How does synchronized solve it?", "What is deadlock?" and "Explain wait(), notify() and notifyAll()".

Recap: Threads let one program do several things at once while sharing memory. Create them by extending Thread or, preferably, implementing Runnable, and always call start(). Execution order is unpredictable, threads move through states from new to terminated, and sleep and join control timing. Shared mutable data causes race conditions, which synchronized methods and blocks prevent using each object's lock; wait and notify coordinate threads, and consistent lock ordering avoids deadlock. Next, we revisit OOP in C++, where many of these ideas look different.
key_points: A thread is a unit of execution inside a process; threads share the heap but have their own stacks.
Create threads by extending Thread or (preferably) implementing Runnable / using a lambda.
Call start() to create a new thread; calling run() directly runs in the current thread.
Thread order is unpredictable; states are NEW, RUNNABLE, BLOCKED, WAITING, TIMED_WAITING, TERMINATED.
sleep pauses the current thread; join waits for another thread to finish.
A race condition happens when unsynchronized threads update shared data (count++ is not atomic).
synchronized methods/blocks use an object's lock so only one thread enters the critical section.
Deadlock: threads wait for each other's locks forever; prevent it with a consistent lock order.
lessons.tip: Every time two threads touch the same object, ask: who reads it, who writes it, and what lock protects it? If you cannot answer, there is a race condition waiting.
lessons.task: Write a Counter with increment(), start two threads that each call it 100,000 times, join both and print the count. Run it a few times without synchronized, then add synchronized and compare.

quiz.q: Which call actually creates a new thread of execution?
quiz.explain: start() asks the JVM to create a thread that then calls run().

quiz.q: Why is implementing Runnable usually preferred over extending Thread?
options: The class can still extend another class and task is separate from thread
Runnable threads never have race conditions
quiz.explain: Java allows only one superclass, so Runnable keeps inheritance free.

quiz.q: Two threads each do count++ 1000 times without synchronization. The result:
quiz.explain: count++ is read-modify-write, so updates can be lost in a race.

quiz.q: What does the synchronized keyword use to protect code?
quiz.explain: A thread must hold the object's lock to enter.

quiz.q: Thread A holds lock X and waits for Y; thread B holds Y and waits for X. This is:
options: Starvation of the main thread only
quiz.explain: Each waits forever for the other: deadlock.

lessons.title: OOP in C++
lessons.content:
If you have learned to ride a bicycle in Rajshahi, you can ride one in Sylhet; the pedals, brakes and balance are the same, even if the roads look different. OOP is the same in Java and C++: classes, objects, encapsulation, inheritance and polymorphism all exist in both. But C++ gives you more direct control, especially over memory, and has some features Java left out on purpose, such as destructors, multiple inheritance and friend functions. Many Bangladeshi universities, including BUET and KUET style syllabuses, teach OOP with C++, so this lesson walks through OOP the C++ way and compares it with Java.

C++ in one line: C++ was created by Bjarne Stroustrup starting around 1979 as "C with Classes", and was renamed C++ in 1983. It compiles directly to machine code, with no virtual machine and no garbage collector by default. That makes it fast and close to the hardware, which is why it is used in games, operating systems, embedded devices and competitive programming, but it also means the programmer is responsible for memory.

Declaring a class: class Student { private: string name; int roll; public: Student(string n, int r) { name = n; roll = r; } void show() { cout << name << " " << roll << endl; } };. Notice three differences from Java. Access specifiers are written as labelled sections, private: and public:, not on every member. The class ends with a semicolon after the closing brace, which beginners often forget. And members of a class are private by default if you write no label.

class versus struct: In C++, struct and class are almost identical; both can have members, functions, constructors and inheritance. The only difference is the default access: members of a struct are public by default, while members of a class are private by default. By convention, struct is used for simple data bundles and class for full objects with behaviour.

Defining member functions outside the class: Larger classes usually declare functions inside the class and define them outside using the scope resolution operator ::. class Account { double balance; public: void deposit(double amt); }; void Account::deposit(double amt) { if (amt > 0) balance += amt; }. Often the class declaration goes in a header file Account.h and the definitions in Account.cpp. Account::deposit reads as "the deposit that belongs to Account".

Objects on the stack and on the heap: In Java every object is created with new on the heap. In C++ you can create objects directly as local variables: Student s("Rahim", 101); s.show();. This object lives on the stack and is destroyed automatically when the enclosing block ends. You can also create one on the heap: Student* p = new Student("Fatima", 102); p->show(); delete p;. Here p is a pointer, members are reached with the arrow operator ->, and the programmer must call delete, or the memory leaks.

Constructors and initializer lists: C++ constructors look like Java's, but C++ prefers a member initializer list to set fields: Student(string n, int r) : name(n), roll(r) { }. The list after the colon initializes members directly before the constructor body runs. It is required for const members, reference members and base classes without default constructors, and it is usually more efficient. Constructors can be overloaded and can have default arguments, such as Student(string n = "Unknown", int r = 0).

Destructors: A destructor is a special member function with the class name preceded by a tilde, ~Student(), no parameters and no return type. It runs automatically when an object is destroyed: when a stack object goes out of scope, or when delete is called on a heap object. It is used to release resources: free memory allocated with new, close files, release locks. Destructors run in the reverse order of construction. Java has no destructors (lesson 5), because its garbage collector frees memory at unpredictable times.

RAII, the C++ way of managing resources: Because destructors run at a predictable moment, C++ ties resources to object lifetime, an idiom called RAII (Resource Acquisition Is Initialization). A File object opens a file in its constructor and closes it in its destructor; as soon as the object goes out of scope, even because of an exception, the file is closed. Smart pointers such as std::unique_ptr and std::shared_ptr use RAII to delete heap objects automatically, and modern C++ code uses them instead of raw new and delete.

Copy constructor and the shallow copy danger: When you write Student b = a; or pass an object by value to a function, C++ calls the copy constructor. If you do not write one, the compiler generates one that copies each member. That is fine for ints and strings, but if a class holds a raw pointer to heap memory, both copies point to the same memory, and when both destructors run, the memory is deleted twice, which is undefined behaviour and often a crash. Such classes need a user-written copy constructor that makes a deep copy, together with a copy assignment operator and a destructor: the "rule of three".

The this pointer: In C++, this is a pointer to the current object, not a reference, so you write this->name = name; with the arrow. Returning *this, the object itself, allows chaining as in Java's fluent style.

Inheritance syntax: class CSEStudent : public Student { string lang; public: CSEStudent(string n, int r, string l) : Student(n, r), lang(l) { } };. The base class constructor is called in the initializer list, the C++ equivalent of Java's super(...). The word public before Student is the inheritance access mode: with public inheritance, public members of the base stay public in the child and protected stay protected. With protected inheritance, public base members become protected; with private inheritance, they become private. Almost all is-a relationships use public inheritance.

Overriding needs virtual: This is the biggest difference from Java. In Java, all non-static, non-private, non-final methods are dispatched dynamically. In C++, a member function is dispatched dynamically only if it is declared virtual in the base class. class Animal { public: virtual void sound() { cout << "..."; } }; class Dog : public Animal { public: void sound() override { cout << "Woof"; } };. Then Animal* a = new Dog(); a->sound(); prints Woof. If sound were not virtual, a->sound() would call Animal's version, because the pointer type decides: static binding.

Polymorphism works through pointers and references: In C++, runtime polymorphism only happens when you call through a base pointer or base reference, such as Animal* or Animal&. If you assign a Dog to a plain Animal variable, Animal x = Dog();, the Dog part is cut off and only the Animal part is copied. This is called object slicing, and x.sound() will call Animal's version. Java avoids slicing because Java variables always hold references.

How virtual works, the vtable: Compilers typically implement virtual functions with a virtual table, or vtable, for each class that has virtual functions, holding pointers to that class's versions of each virtual function. Each object of such a class carries a hidden pointer, often called the vptr, to its class's vtable. A virtual call follows the object's vptr to the table and jumps to the right function. This costs a little memory per object and a small extra step per call, which is why C++ makes virtual optional. The C++ standard does not require vtables, but practically all compilers use them.

Virtual destructors: If you delete a derived object through a base pointer, Animal* a = new Dog(); delete a;, and Animal's destructor is not virtual, only Animal's destructor runs, and the behaviour is undefined; Dog's resources may leak. The rule: any class meant to be used polymorphically, with virtual functions, should have a virtual destructor: virtual ~Animal() { }.

Pure virtual functions and abstract classes: A pure virtual function is declared with = 0 and has no required body: virtual double area() = 0;. A class with at least one pure virtual function is abstract and cannot be instantiated, exactly like a Java abstract class (lesson 13). A class with only pure virtual functions and a virtual destructor plays the role of a Java interface (lesson 14), since C++ has no separate interface keyword.

Multiple inheritance: C++ allows a class to inherit from several base classes: class SmartPhone : public Phone, public Camera { };. A SmartPhone is both a Phone and a Camera, with members of both. This is powerful but brings ambiguity: if both bases have a member called power(), calling sp.power() is ambiguous, and you must say sp.Phone::power() or sp.Camera::power().

The diamond problem and virtual inheritance: Suppose class Person { string name; }; class Student : public Person { }; class Employee : public Person { }; class TeachingAssistant : public Student, public Employee { };. A TeachingAssistant now contains two separate Person parts, so two names, and ta.name is ambiguous. This is the diamond problem from lesson 10. C++ solves it with virtual inheritance: class Student : virtual public Person and class Employee : virtual public Person. Then TeachingAssistant contains only one shared Person part. Java avoids the whole issue by allowing only single class inheritance.

Friend functions and friend classes: C++ lets a class grant access to its private members to a specific outside function or class by declaring it a friend: class Account { double balance; friend void audit(const Account& a); };. Now the non-member function audit can read a.balance directly. Friends are useful for operators like << (lesson 23) and for tightly coupled helper classes, but they weaken encapsulation, so use them sparingly. Friendship is not inherited and not mutual. Java has no friend feature; the closest is package-private access.

Static members and const member functions: Static members work as in Java (lesson 6), but a static data member is usually declared in the class and defined once outside it, such as int Student::count = 0;. A member function marked const, void show() const, promises not to change the object, and only const functions can be called on const objects. This const-correctness has no direct equivalent in Java and is often tested in C++ exams.

Real life example 1, a shape program in C++: class Shape { public: virtual double area() const = 0; virtual ~Shape() { } }; class Circle : public Shape { double r; public: Circle(double r) : r(r) { } double area() const override { return 3.14159 * r * r; } };. A vector<Shape*> holds circles and rectangles; a loop calls s->area() on each; finally a loop calls delete on each pointer, which runs the right destructor thanks to the virtual destructor. With unique_ptr<Shape> instead of raw pointers, the deletes happen automatically.

Real life example 2, a game engine: Many game engines are written in C++ for speed. A base class GameObject has virtual void update() and virtual void draw(). Player, Enemy and Bullet override them. Each frame, the engine loops over all objects and calls update and draw through base pointers. Bullets that leave the screen are destroyed, and their destructors free their sprite memory immediately, without waiting for any garbage collector, which keeps frame times smooth.

Common mistakes: Forgetting the semicolon after a class. Forgetting virtual and wondering why the base version runs. Missing a virtual destructor in a polymorphic base class. Object slicing by passing objects by value instead of by reference or pointer. Forgetting delete or deleting twice. Relying on the default copy constructor for classes with raw pointers. Using friends to bypass good design.

What exams ask: "Differentiate between class and struct in C++", "What is a destructor? When is it called?", "What is a virtual function? How does it achieve runtime polymorphism?", "What is a pure virtual function and an abstract class?", "Why do we need a virtual destructor?", "What is the diamond problem and how does virtual inheritance solve it?", "What is a friend function?" and "Compare OOP in C++ and Java".

Recap: C++ supports the same OOP pillars as Java with different syntax and more control. Classes default to private, objects can live on the stack or heap, and destructors with RAII manage resources deterministically. Overriding needs virtual for runtime polymorphism, which works through pointers and references, usually implemented with vtables, and polymorphic bases need virtual destructors. Pure virtual functions create abstract classes. C++ allows multiple inheritance, solving the diamond problem with virtual inheritance, and friend functions can access private members. Next, C++ operator overloading and templates.
key_points: C++ class members are private by default; struct members are public by default.
Objects can live on the stack (auto-destroyed) or heap (new/delete); heap members use ->.
Constructors use initializer lists; destructors (~Class) run automatically at end of lifetime (RAII).
Default copy is member-wise (shallow); classes with raw pointers need the rule of three.
Runtime polymorphism needs virtual functions and works through pointers/references; values cause slicing.
Polymorphic base classes need a virtual destructor; virtual calls are typically implemented with vtables.
Pure virtual (= 0) makes a class abstract; such classes act as interfaces.
C++ allows multiple inheritance; virtual inheritance fixes the diamond; friends can access private members.
lessons.tip: When reading C++ OOP code, look for the word virtual first. It tells you which calls are decided at runtime and which are fixed at compile time.
lessons.task: In C++ write class Animal with virtual void sound() and a virtual destructor, and two derived classes. Store them in a vector<Animal*>, call sound() in a loop, then remove the word virtual and compare the output.

quiz.q: What is the default access of members in a C++ class?
quiz.explain: class defaults to private; struct defaults to public.

quiz.q: When is a C++ destructor of a stack object called?
options: When the object goes out of scope
quiz.explain: Stack objects are destroyed automatically at the end of their block.

quiz.q: Animal* a = new Dog(); a->sound(); prints Animal's version. Why?
options: sound() is not declared virtual in Animal
quiz.explain: Without virtual, C++ uses static binding based on the pointer type.

quiz.q: How does C++ avoid two copies of a common base in the diamond problem?
quiz.explain: class B : virtual public A shares one A sub-object.

quiz.q: A class with virtual double area() = 0; is:
quiz.explain: A pure virtual function makes the class abstract.

lessons.title: C++ Operator Overloading and Templates
lessons.content:
When you add 5 + 3 you get 8. When you "add" two strings in many languages, "Dhaka" + "City", you get "DhakaCity". The same + sign does different jobs depending on what it is applied to. Now imagine a Money class for taka and paisa, a Fraction class, or a Matrix class. Would it not be natural to write total = price1 + price2 or c = a * b, just like with numbers? C++ allows exactly this through operator overloading. It also allows you to write one function or class that works for any type through templates. Both are classic topics in C++ based OOP courses.

What operator overloading is: Operator overloading lets you define what an operator such as +, -, ==, <, << or [] means when its operands are objects of your class. It is a form of compile-time polymorphism (lesson 12): the same symbol, different behaviour depending on types. Under the hood an overloaded operator is just a function with a special name: operator+, operator==, operator<< and so on. a + b becomes a call to operator+(a, b) or a.operator+(b).

A first example, a Money class: class Money { int paisa; public: Money(int taka, int p) : paisa(taka * 100 + p) { } Money operator+(const Money& other) const { Money r(0, 0); r.paisa = paisa + other.paisa; return r; } };. Now Money a(120, 50), b(30, 75); Money c = a + b; gives 151 taka 25 paisa. Notice the parameter is passed by const reference, to avoid copying and to promise not to change it, and the function is const because adding does not change a.

Member versus non-member operators: An operator can be written as a member function, where the left operand is the object itself (this) and the right operand is the parameter, or as a non-member function taking both operands as parameters. Money operator+(const Money& a, const Money& b) as a non-member works the same. Non-members are needed when the left operand is not your class, for example when you want 2 * money or cout << money. If a non-member needs private fields, it is often declared a friend (lesson 22).

Overloading << for printing: To write cout << m;, define a non-member function: ostream& operator<<(ostream& out, const Money& m) { out << "Tk " << m.paisa / 100 << "." << m.paisa % 100; return out; }, declared as friend inside Money so it can read paisa. It must be a non-member because the left operand is the ostream, not a Money. It returns the stream by reference so that chaining works: cout << a << " and " << b << endl;. This is the C++ equivalent of overriding toString in Java (lesson 15).

Comparison operators: bool operator==(const Money& o) const { return paisa == o.paisa; } and bool operator<(const Money& o) const { return paisa < o.paisa; }. Defining operator< lets you sort a vector of Money objects with std::sort, which uses < by default, similar to implementing Comparable in Java (lesson 19). Since C++20, the three-way comparison operator <=>, nicknamed the spaceship operator, can generate all the relational operators at once.

Increment operators, prefix and postfix: ++ comes in two forms. Prefix ++x increments and returns the new value; postfix x++ increments but returns the old value. C++ tells them apart with a dummy int parameter: Counter& operator++() { ++count; return *this; } for prefix, and Counter operator++(int) { Counter old = *this; ++count; return old; } for postfix. The prefix version returns a reference and avoids a copy, which is why experienced C++ programmers prefer ++it in loops.

The subscript operator: Overloading [] lets your class behave like an array. class Marks { int m[5]; public: int& operator[](int i) { if (i < 0 || i >= 5) throw out_of_range("bad index"); return m[i]; } };. Because it returns a reference, marks[2] = 85; changes the stored value. Adding a bounds check gives the safety Java arrays have by default (lesson 2).

The assignment operator: a = b; calls operator=. The compiler provides a default that copies each member, which causes the same shallow copy problem as the default copy constructor when the class owns raw pointers (lesson 22). A user-written version should check for self-assignment, copy the data deeply and return *this by reference so that a = b = c works. This is part of the rule of three.

Rules and limits of operator overloading: You cannot invent new operators such as ** or <>. You cannot change an operator's precedence, its associativity or the number of operands it takes. At least one operand must be a user-defined type, so you cannot change what + means for two ints. Some operators cannot be overloaded at all: the scope operator ::, the member access operator ., the pointer-to-member operator .*, the conditional operator ?: and sizeof. And =, [], () and -> must be member functions.

Use operator overloading wisely: Overload an operator only when its meaning is obvious and matches what people expect. + for adding money, == for equality and << for printing are natural. Using + to delete a record or * to send an email would confuse every reader. Java deliberately does not allow programmers to overload operators, to avoid such confusion; only String gets the built-in + for concatenation.

A worked Complex number example: class Complex { double re, im; public: Complex(double r = 0, double i = 0) : re(r), im(i) { } Complex operator+(const Complex& o) const { return Complex(re + o.re, im + o.im); } Complex operator*(const Complex& o) const { return Complex(re * o.re - im * o.im, re * o.im + im * o.re); } friend ostream& operator<<(ostream& out, const Complex& c) { return out << c.re << " + " << c.im << "i"; } };. With a(1, 2) and b(3, 4), a + b prints 4 + 6i, and a * b prints -5 + 10i, because (1)(3) - (2)(4) = -5 and (1)(4) + (2)(3) = 10. This Complex class is probably the single most common operator overloading exam question.

Templates, the idea: Suppose you need a function that returns the larger of two values, for ints, doubles, strings and Money. Writing four almost identical functions is boring and error-prone. A template is a blueprint from which the compiler generates functions or classes for each type you use. It is C++'s way of writing generic code, similar in purpose to Java generics (lesson 18), but working differently inside.

Function templates: template <typename T> T maxOf(T a, T b) { return (a > b) ? a : b; }. Then maxOf(3, 7) returns 7, maxOf(2.5, 1.5) returns 2.5, and maxOf(string("apple"), string("mango")) returns "mango". The compiler deduces T from the arguments. The keyword class can be used instead of typename in the template parameter list with the same meaning. The only requirement on T is that the operations used, here >, exist for it; for Money that means operator> must be overloaded.

Class templates: template <typename T> class Stack { vector<T> items; public: void push(const T& x) { items.push_back(x); } T pop() { T top = items.back(); items.pop_back(); return top; } bool empty() const { return items.empty(); } };. Stack<int> s1; Stack<string> s2; each create a separate stack type. Templates can have several parameters, such as template <typename K, typename V> class Pair, and even non-type parameters such as template <typename T, int N> class FixedArray, where N is a compile-time constant size.

How templates work, instantiation: When you use Stack<int>, the compiler generates a real class from the template with T replaced by int; this is called template instantiation. Stack<string> generates another class. So unlike Java's type erasure, C++ templates produce separate code for each type, which makes them fast and allows primitives like int directly, but can make programs larger and compile errors longer. Because the compiler must see the whole template to instantiate it, templates are usually written entirely in header files.

Template specialization: Sometimes one type needs a different implementation. You can provide a specialized version: template <> const char* maxOf<const char*>(const char* a, const char* b) { return strcmp(a, b) > 0 ? a : b; }. Without this, comparing two C-style strings with > would compare their memory addresses, not their text. Specialization lets the general template handle most types while special cases get correct handling.

The Standard Template Library: The STL is C++'s library of templates, roughly the C++ counterpart of Java's Collections Framework (lesson 19). Containers: vector (dynamic array, like ArrayList), list (doubly linked list), deque, set and map (usually balanced trees, sorted, like TreeSet and TreeMap), unordered_set and unordered_map (hash tables, like HashSet and HashMap), stack, queue and priority_queue. Iterators: objects that point into containers, used with begin() and end(). Algorithms: sort, find, count, reverse, binary_search and many more, which work on any container through iterators.

Using the STL with your classes: vector<Money> bills = {Money(100, 0), Money(45, 50), Money(250, 0)}; sort(bills.begin(), bills.end()); works because Money has operator<. map<string, Money> dues; dues["Rahim"] = Money(500, 0); stores amounts by name. You can also pass a custom comparison as a lambda: sort(v.begin(), v.end(), [](const Student& a, const Student& b) { return a.cgpa > b.cgpa; });, just like a Java Comparator.

Real life example 1, a fraction calculator for school maths: class Fraction { int num, den; ... }. Overloading +, -, *, / with reduction by the greatest common divisor, == for comparison and << for printing means a student's program can write Fraction a(1, 2), b(1, 3); cout << a + b; and see 5/6. The code reads like the maths in the textbook, which is the real goal of operator overloading.

Real life example 2, a generic leaderboard: template <typename T> class Leaderboard { vector<pair<string, T>> entries; ... } can rank cricket batters by runs (Leaderboard<int>), runners by time (Leaderboard<double>) or quiz teams by a custom Score class with operator< overloaded. The ranking logic, sorting and printing the top 10, is written once. Competitive programmers in Bangladesh use STL containers and algorithms like these every day on platforms such as Codeforces.

Common mistakes: Overloading << as a member function. Forgetting to return the stream, which breaks chaining. Mixing up prefix and postfix ++ signatures. Returning a reference to a local variable from an operator. Trying to overload :: or sizeof. Putting template definitions in a .cpp file and getting linker errors. Using a template with a type that lacks the required operator.

What exams ask: "What is operator overloading? Which operators cannot be overloaded?", "Overload + for a Complex or Money class", "Why is << overloaded as a friend function?", "Differentiate between overloading prefix and postfix ++", "What is a function template? A class template?", "What is template specialization?", "Compare C++ templates with Java generics" and "What are the components of the STL?".

Recap: Operator overloading gives operators meaning for your classes through functions named operator+, operator<< and so on, written as members or non-members (often friends), within strict rules about which operators and what can change. Templates let one function or class work for many types; the compiler instantiates separate code for each type, unlike Java's erasure, and specialization handles special cases. The STL provides template containers, iterators and algorithms. Next, we return to Java to build graphical user interfaces with events.
key_points: Operator overloading defines operators for your classes via functions named operator+, operator<<, etc.
Operators can be members (left operand is this) or non-members (often friends).
<< must be a non-member returning ostream& so chaining works.
Postfix ++ takes a dummy int parameter; prefix returns a reference.
You cannot overload ::, ., .*, ?: or sizeof, invent operators, or change precedence/arity.
Templates (template <typename T>) generate code for each type used: instantiation.
Unlike Java's erasure, C++ templates create separate code per type and allow primitives; specialization handles special types.
The STL offers template containers (vector, map, set...), iterators and algorithms (sort, find...).
lessons.tip: Overload an operator only if a reader would guess its meaning without looking. If you need a comment to explain it, use a named function instead.
lessons.task: In C++ write a Fraction class with overloaded +, == and <<, reducing results by the GCD. Then write template <typename T> T maxOf(T a, T b) and test it with int, double and string.

quiz.q: Which operator cannot be overloaded in C++?
quiz.explain: The scope resolution operator :: cannot be overloaded.

quiz.q: Why is operator<< for printing a non-member function?
options: Its left operand is the ostream, not your class
quiz.explain: In cout << obj, the left operand is cout.

quiz.q: How does C++ distinguish postfix x++ from prefix ++x when overloading?
options: Postfix takes a dummy int parameter
quiz.explain: operator++(int) is postfix; operator++() is prefix.

quiz.q: How do C++ templates differ from Java generics?
options: C++ instantiates separate code per type; Java erases types
Java instantiates code per type; C++ erases
quiz.explain: Templates are expanded per type at compile time.

quiz.q: Which STL container is most like Java's ArrayList?
quiz.explain: vector is a dynamic array with fast index access.

lessons.title: GUI and Event-Driven Programming
lessons.content:
Think about a doorbell. The bell does nothing most of the time. It just waits. When a guest presses the button, the bell rings. The bell does not keep asking "has anyone pressed me yet?" in a loop; it reacts when the event happens. Apps with buttons, text boxes and menus work the same way. The program sets up the screen, then waits, and runs a piece of code whenever the user clicks, types or taps. This style is called event-driven programming, and building graphical user interfaces (GUIs) in Java is a great showcase of everything you have learned about objects, interfaces and polymorphism.

Console programs versus GUI programs: The programs you have written so far follow a fixed sequence: read input, process, print output, end. The program is in control. A GUI program flips this around. It creates windows and components, registers what should happen for each event, and then hands control to an event loop. From then on the user is in control, and the program responds to whatever they do, in any order.

Java's GUI toolkits: Java has had three main GUI libraries. AWT (Abstract Window Toolkit) was the first, from 1995, and uses the operating system's own components. Swing, in the javax.swing package, came next; it draws its own components in Java, so it looks the same everywhere, and its class names usually start with J, such as JFrame and JButton. JavaFX is the newer toolkit with CSS styling and better graphics; since Java 11 it is distributed separately as OpenJFX. Many university courses teach Swing because it ships with the JDK, and some teach JavaFX. The ideas are the same in both.

Components and containers: A GUI is built from components, the visible pieces: buttons (JButton), labels (JLabel), text fields (JTextField), password fields (JPasswordField), check boxes (JCheckBox), combo boxes (JComboBox) and text areas (JTextArea). Containers hold components: JFrame is a top-level window, and JPanel is a general-purpose box that can hold components and other panels. Containers can be nested, so a complex screen is a tree of panels and components. This is the composition idea from lesson 9: a window has panels, a panel has buttons.

The component hierarchy as OOP: In Swing, JButton, JLabel and JTextField all extend JComponent, which extends Container, which extends Component. Because of inheritance, every component has methods like setVisible, setEnabled, setBackground and setToolTipText. Because of polymorphism, a panel can hold any Component in its list and ask each one to paint itself. The library is one of the largest real examples of the class hierarchies you studied in lessons 10 to 13.

A first window: JFrame f = new JFrame("Taka Converter"); f.setSize(350, 150); f.setDefaultCloseOperation(JFrame.EXIT_ON_CLOSE); f.setLayout(new FlowLayout()); f.add(new JLabel("Hello, Bangladesh!")); f.setVisible(true);. setDefaultCloseOperation makes the program end when the window is closed; without it, closing the window only hides it and the program keeps running. setVisible(true) shows the window, and it should be called after adding the components.

Layout managers: Instead of placing each component at exact pixel positions, which breaks when the window resizes or fonts change, Java uses layout managers that arrange components automatically. FlowLayout places components left to right in a row, wrapping like words in a paragraph; it is the default for JPanel. BorderLayout divides the container into five areas, NORTH, SOUTH, EAST, WEST and CENTER; it is the default for a JFrame's content pane. GridLayout makes a grid of equal cells, perfect for a calculator keypad: new GridLayout(4, 4). Panels with different layouts can be nested to build almost any screen.

The event model: Swing uses the delegation event model with three roles. The event source is the component where something happens, such as a button. The event object describes what happened, such as an ActionEvent, carrying details like which component fired it. The event listener is an object that wants to be told, and it implements a listener interface such as ActionListener, which has a single method actionPerformed(ActionEvent e). You connect them by registering the listener with the source: button.addActionListener(listener);. When the user clicks, the source calls actionPerformed on every registered listener.

A complete small example: JTextField takaField = new JTextField(10); JButton convert = new JButton("Convert"); JLabel result = new JLabel("USD: "); convert.addActionListener(e -> { try { double taka = Double.parseDouble(takaField.getText()); result.setText("USD: " + String.format("%.2f", taka / rate)); } catch (NumberFormatException ex) { result.setText("Please enter a number"); } });. Here the listener is written as a lambda, which works because ActionListener is a functional interface (lesson 14). The exception handling from lesson 17 protects against bad input.

Three ways to write listeners: You can write a separate named class that implements ActionListener, which is clear for complex handlers that are reused. You can write an anonymous inner class, new ActionListener() { public void actionPerformed(ActionEvent e) { ... } }, which was common before Java 8 and is still seen in older textbooks. Or you can use a lambda, which is the shortest and most common in modern code. All three create an object that implements the same interface, so the button treats them identically: polymorphism again.

Other kinds of events: ActionListener handles button clicks and pressing Enter in a text field. MouseListener handles mouse presses, releases, clicks, entering and exiting a component. KeyListener handles key presses. WindowListener handles opening and closing windows. ItemListener handles check boxes and combo boxes. Interfaces like MouseListener have several methods; if you only care about one, extend an adapter class such as MouseAdapter, which provides empty versions of all of them, and override just the one you need, such as mouseClicked.

Dialogs for quick messages: JOptionPane provides ready-made dialog boxes. JOptionPane.showMessageDialog(frame, "Saved successfully"); shows a message. JOptionPane.showConfirmDialog(frame, "Delete this record?") returns which button was pressed, such as YES_OPTION. JOptionPane.showInputDialog(frame, "Enter your roll:") returns the typed text, or null if the user cancels. These are modal dialogs: the user must close them before using the main window again, which is right for confirmations and errors.

Writing a listener as a separate class, worked example: class ConvertHandler implements ActionListener { private final JTextField in; private final JLabel out; ConvertHandler(JTextField in, JLabel out) { this.in = in; this.out = out; } public void actionPerformed(ActionEvent e) { out.setText("Length: " + in.getText().length()); } }. Then button.addActionListener(new ConvertHandler(field, label));. The handler receives the components it needs through its constructor, which is composition (lesson 9). The same handler class can be attached to several buttons, and e.getSource() tells it which one was clicked.

The event dispatch thread: Swing uses one special thread, the event dispatch thread (EDT), to handle all events and to update components. Swing components are not thread-safe (lesson 21), so they should only be touched from the EDT. Start your GUI on it with SwingUtilities.invokeLater(() -> createAndShowGui());. And never run slow work, such as downloading a file or a long calculation, directly inside an event handler, because it blocks the EDT and the whole window freezes. Use a background thread, for example a SwingWorker, and update the components back on the EDT when the work finishes.

The Observer pattern behind events: The event model is a classic design pattern called Observer (lesson 25). The subject, here the button, keeps a list of observers, the listeners, and notifies all of them when its state changes. The subject does not know or care what the listeners do; it only knows they implement the listener interface. This loose coupling (lesson 14) means you can add a second listener that logs every click without touching the first one.

Model-View-Controller: As GUIs grow, mixing calculation code into event handlers makes a mess. The MVC idea separates three roles. The Model holds the data and rules, for example a Converter class with a rate and a convert method, knowing nothing about windows. The View displays the data, the frame, fields and labels. The Controller handles user input, receiving events from the View, calling the Model and updating the View. With MVC you can test the Model without any GUI, and you could replace a Swing view with a JavaFX or Android view while keeping the same Model.

JavaFX in brief: JavaFX uses a theatre metaphor. A Stage is the window, a Scene is the content shown on the stage, and the scene holds a tree of nodes such as Button, Label, TextField and layout panes like VBox, HBox and GridPane. Event handling is similar: button.setOnAction(e -> label.setText("Clicked!"));. A JavaFX program extends the Application class and overrides its start(Stage stage) method, an example of the template method idea from lesson 13. JavaFX can also be styled with CSS and laid out with FXML files.

Real life example 1, a GPA calculator for students: The window has a JComboBox for each course's grade, a JTextField for credits, and a Calculate button. The Model class GpaCalculator holds a list of (credit, grade point) pairs and computes the weighted average: for 3 credits with 4.0 and 3 credits with 3.5, (12 + 10.5) / 6 = 3.75. The button's listener reads the inputs, calls the model and shows "Your GPA: 3.75" in a JLabel. Invalid credits trigger a friendly message through a JOptionPane dialog instead of a crash.

Real life example 2, a small shop's billing screen: A JTable lists items, a JTextField scans or types product codes, and buttons for Add, Remove and Print. Pressing Enter in the code field fires an ActionEvent that looks up the product in a HashMap (lesson 19) and adds a row. A Print button writes the bill to a text file (lesson 20). Because the cash drawer printer can be slow, printing runs on a background thread so the cashier can keep scanning the next customer's items.

Common mistakes: Forgetting setVisible(true) or calling it before adding components. Forgetting setDefaultCloseOperation, so the program keeps running after the window closes. Using absolute positions that break on other screens. Doing long tasks inside actionPerformed and freezing the GUI. Updating Swing components from a background thread. Putting all the logic inside listeners instead of a separate model class.

What exams ask: "What is event-driven programming?", "Explain the delegation event model with an example", "What is a listener? Name some listener interfaces", "Differentiate between AWT and Swing", "What are layout managers? Explain FlowLayout, BorderLayout and GridLayout", "What is an adapter class?" and "Write a Swing program with a text field and a button that shows the square of the entered number".

Recap: GUI programs are event-driven: they build a tree of components inside containers, arrange them with layout managers, and react to events. In the delegation event model, a source fires an event object to registered listeners, which implement interfaces like ActionListener, often written as lambdas or adapters. Swing's components form a big class hierarchy, events follow the Observer pattern, all GUI updates belong on the event dispatch thread, slow work belongs on background threads, and MVC keeps logic separate from screens. In the final lesson, we bring everything together with object oriented design principles and patterns.
key_points: Event-driven programs set up the screen, then react to user events through an event loop.
Java GUI toolkits: AWT (oldest), Swing (javax.swing, J-classes), JavaFX (newer, separate since Java 11).
Components (JButton, JLabel, JTextField) live in containers (JFrame, JPanel), forming a tree.
Layout managers: FlowLayout (JPanel default), BorderLayout (JFrame default), GridLayout.
Delegation event model: source fires an event object to registered listeners (addActionListener).
Listeners can be named classes, anonymous classes, lambdas, or adapter subclasses.
Update Swing only on the event dispatch thread; run slow work in the background.
The event model is the Observer pattern; MVC separates model, view and controller.
lessons.tip: Keep event handlers short: read the input, call a model method, show the result. If a handler grows beyond ten lines, move the logic into a model class.
lessons.task: Write a Swing program with a JTextField, a JButton and a JLabel. When the button is clicked, show the square of the entered number, or 'Please enter a number' if the input is invalid.

quiz.q: In the delegation event model, what is the JButton that gets clicked?
quiz.explain: The component where the event happens is the source.

quiz.q: Which method must an ActionListener implement?
quiz.explain: ActionListener has a single method, actionPerformed.

quiz.q: Which layout manager is the default for a JFrame's content pane?
quiz.explain: JFrame uses BorderLayout; JPanel uses FlowLayout.

quiz.q: Why should a long download not run inside actionPerformed?
options: It blocks the event dispatch thread and freezes the GUI
quiz.explain: Slow work belongs on a background thread.

quiz.q: What is an adapter class such as MouseAdapter for?
options: Providing empty listener methods so you override only the ones you need
quiz.explain: It saves writing empty bodies for unused interface methods.

lessons.title: Object Oriented Design: UML, SOLID and Design Patterns
lessons.content:
Knowing how to use a hammer, a saw and nails does not make you an architect. To build a good house, you need a plan: where the rooms go, how the plumbing connects, where the load-bearing walls stand. Over the last 24 lessons you collected OOP tools: classes, encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism, interfaces, exceptions, collections and more. This final lesson is about using them well: drawing designs with UML class diagrams, following the SOLID principles, and reusing proven solutions called design patterns. It ends with a recap of the whole course and what to learn next.

UML class diagrams: UML (Unified Modeling Language) is a standard visual language for describing software designs. The class diagram is the most used UML diagram in OOP courses. Each class is a box with three compartments: the class name at the top, attributes in the middle and operations (methods) at the bottom. Abstract class names are written in italics or marked {abstract}, and interfaces are marked with <<interface>> above the name.

Visibility and types in UML: Each member is prefixed with a visibility symbol: + for public, - for private, # for protected and ~ for package. Types are written after a colon. For example: - balance : double, + deposit(amount : double) : void, + getBalance() : double. Static members are underlined. So a class box for Account tells a reader at a glance what the class stores and offers, and what it hides.

Relationships in UML: A plain solid line is an association, optionally with an arrowhead for direction and multiplicities like 1, 0..1, * or 1..* at the ends (lesson 9). A hollow diamond at the whole's end marks aggregation; a filled diamond marks composition. A solid line with a hollow triangle pointing at the parent is inheritance (generalization). A dashed line with a hollow triangle pointing at the interface is realization, meaning a class implements an interface. A dashed arrow is a dependency. Exams often ask you to draw a small system with all of these.

A worked UML example: For a library: Library has a filled diamond to Book? No; books can move between branches, so it is a hollow diamond, aggregation, with multiplicity 1 on Library and * on Book. Book has a filled diamond to Page, composition. Member and Book are associated through Loan, with 1 Member to * Loans and 1 Book to * Loans over time. StudentMember and TeacherMember inherit from an abstract Member, drawn with hollow triangles. And Member realizes an interface Notifiable, drawn with a dashed line and hollow triangle. Practising one such diagram by hand prepares you for most design questions.

The SOLID principles: SOLID is a set of five design principles, popularized by Robert C. Martin, that help keep object oriented code easy to change. S is Single Responsibility, O is Open-Closed, L is Liskov Substitution, I is Interface Segregation and D is Dependency Inversion. Each one addresses a common way designs go wrong.

S, Single Responsibility Principle: A class should have one reason to change, meaning one job. Imagine a Report class that calculates results, formats them as text and saves them to a file. A change in the file format, the text layout or the GPA rules would all force changes to the same class. Better: ResultCalculator calculates, ReportFormatter formats, ReportSaver saves. Each class becomes smaller, easier to test and safer to change.

O, Open-Closed Principle: Software entities should be open for extension but closed for modification. You should be able to add new behaviour without editing tested code. Lesson 12 showed this: a loop that calls shape.area() handles any new Shape subclass without changes, while a long if-else chain on shape types must be edited for every new shape. Polymorphism and interfaces are the main tools for following this principle.

L, Liskov Substitution Principle: Named after computer scientist Barbara Liskov, it says that objects of a subclass must be usable wherever the parent is expected, without breaking correct behaviour. The classic violation is Square extends Rectangle: code that sets a rectangle's width to 5 and height to 4 and expects area 20 gets 16 if the object is a Square that keeps its sides equal. If a child cannot honour the parent's promises, the inheritance is wrong, even if "a square is a rectangle" sounds true in maths.

I, Interface Segregation Principle: Clients should not be forced to depend on methods they do not use. A huge interface Machine { print(); scan(); fax(); staple(); } forces a simple printer to implement fax and staple with empty or error-throwing bodies. Better: small interfaces Printer, Scanner and Fax, and a multifunction machine implements all three while a basic printer implements only Printer. Java's many small functional interfaces follow this idea.

D, Dependency Inversion Principle: High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules; both should depend on abstractions. An OrderService that creates new BkashGateway() inside itself is tied to bKash forever. Instead, OrderService should depend on a PaymentGateway interface (lesson 14) and receive the real gateway from outside, usually through its constructor: new OrderService(new BkashGateway()). This technique of passing dependencies in is called dependency injection, and it makes testing with a fake gateway easy.

Design patterns: A design pattern is a general, reusable solution to a problem that keeps appearing in software design, described in a way you can adapt to your own code. The famous 1994 book "Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software" by Gamma, Helm, Johnson and Vlissides, known as the Gang of Four (GoF), catalogued 23 patterns in three groups: creational patterns (how objects are created), structural patterns (how classes and objects are combined) and behavioural patterns (how objects communicate). You have already met some of them: Template Method (lesson 13), Decorator (lesson 20) and Observer (lesson 24).

Singleton pattern (creational): Singleton ensures a class has only one instance and provides a global access point to it. class AppConfig { private static AppConfig instance; private AppConfig() { } public static AppConfig getInstance() { if (instance == null) instance = new AppConfig(); return instance; } }. The private constructor (lesson 5) stops other classes from using new, and the static method (lesson 6) returns the single object. This simple version is not thread-safe (lesson 21); a common fix is to create the instance eagerly, private static final AppConfig INSTANCE = new AppConfig();. Use Singleton sparingly, because it behaves like a global variable and makes testing harder.

Factory pattern (creational): A factory hides the details of which concrete class to create. interface Notification { void send(String msg); } with classes SmsNotification, EmailNotification and PushNotification. class NotificationFactory { static Notification create(String type) { switch (type) { case "sms": return new SmsNotification(); case "email": return new EmailNotification(); default: return new PushNotification(); } } }. The calling code writes Notification n = NotificationFactory.create(userPreference); n.send("Your order is on the way");, depending only on the interface. This simple form is often called a simple factory; the GoF Factory Method pattern lets subclasses decide which class to create.

Observer pattern (behavioural): Observer defines a one-to-many relationship: when one object, the subject, changes state, all its registered observers are notified automatically. interface PriceObserver { void priceChanged(String item, double price); } class Product { private List<PriceObserver> observers = new ArrayList<>(); void addObserver(PriceObserver o) { observers.add(o); } void setPrice(double p) { price = p; for (PriceObserver o : observers) o.priceChanged(name, p); } }. A wishlist screen, an email alert service and a price history logger can all observe the same product without the Product class knowing anything about them. Java's GUI listeners in lesson 24 are exactly this pattern.

Strategy pattern (behavioural): Strategy defines a family of interchangeable algorithms, each in its own class behind a common interface, so the algorithm can be chosen at runtime. interface DeliveryFee { double calculate(double km); } with classes NormalFee, ExpressFee and FreeFee (as in lesson 11, but now via composition instead of inheritance). class Checkout { private DeliveryFee fee; void setFee(DeliveryFee f) { fee = f; } double total(double items, double km) { return items + fee.calculate(km); } }. During an Eid campaign the app calls checkout.setFee(new FreeFee()); no Checkout code changes. With lambdas, a strategy can even be written inline: checkout.setFee(km -> 20 + 5 * km);.

Patterns are tools, not goals: Use a pattern when you face the problem it solves, not to make code look clever. A beginner who wraps every class in a factory and every value in a singleton creates more complexity than they remove. Knowing patterns gives you a shared vocabulary: telling a teammate "use a strategy for the fee rules" communicates a whole design in five words.

Course recap, part 1: We began with why OOP exists: keeping data and behaviour together and protecting data (lesson 1), then Java basics (lesson 2). We built classes and objects, references, the stack and the heap (lesson 3), methods and overloading (lesson 4), constructors and object lifetime (lesson 5), and this, static and final (lesson 6). Encapsulation and access modifiers protected our data (lesson 7), strings and wrappers showed immutability in action (lesson 8), and relationships like association, aggregation and composition connected objects (lesson 9).

Course recap, part 2: Inheritance (lesson 10), overriding (lesson 11) and polymorphism (lesson 12) gave us reuse and flexibility, while abstract classes (lesson 13) and interfaces (lesson 14) gave abstraction and contracts. The Object class taught toString, equals and hashCode (lesson 15), packages organised code (lesson 16), exceptions handled errors (lesson 17), generics added type safety (lesson 18) and collections stored groups of objects (lesson 19). File I/O saved data (lesson 20), threads ran tasks at once (lesson 21), C++ showed OOP with destructors, virtual functions, operator overloading and templates (lessons 22 and 23), and GUIs showed event-driven design (lesson 24).

Real life example, designing a small food delivery app: Using everything above: Customer, Restaurant, Rider and Order classes with private fields (encapsulation); Order composed of OrderItems (composition); a PaymentGateway interface with bKash, Nagad and card implementations chosen by a factory (polymorphism, Factory, Dependency Inversion); a DeliveryFee strategy for campaigns (Strategy, Open-Closed); order status updates pushed to the customer's screen and the rider's phone (Observer); orders saved to files or a database with exceptions handled (I/O, exceptions); and a thread pool for handling many orders at once (threads). That is OOP as it is used in real Bangladeshi startups.

Common mistakes: Drawing inheritance arrows the wrong way (they point to the parent). Mixing up aggregation and composition diamonds. Treating SOLID as strict laws instead of guidelines. Using Singleton everywhere. Forcing patterns into code that does not need them. Inheritance that violates Liskov, like Square extends Rectangle.

What exams ask: "Draw a UML class diagram for a given system with visibility and relationships", "Explain the SOLID principles with examples", "What is a design pattern? Classify the GoF patterns", "Implement the Singleton pattern. Is your version thread-safe?", "Explain the Observer pattern with a diagram" and "Differentiate between Strategy and Template Method" (Strategy uses composition and interchangeable objects; Template Method uses inheritance and overridden steps).

What to learn next: Data Structures will show how collections like ArrayList, LinkedList, HashMap and TreeMap work inside, and Algorithms will analyse their speed. Software Engineering will use UML and design patterns on team projects. Database Systems will replace text files with proper storage. And if you want to build apps, Android with Kotlin or Flutter with Dart both use the same OOP ideas you now know. Keep building small projects, a library system, a result portal, a game, because design skill grows by designing.
key_points: UML class boxes show name, attributes and operations with + public, - private, # protected, ~ package.
UML lines: association, hollow diamond aggregation, filled diamond composition, hollow triangle inheritance, dashed triangle realization.
SOLID: Single responsibility, Open-closed, Liskov substitution, Interface segregation, Dependency inversion.
Liskov: a subclass must be usable wherever its parent is expected (Square extends Rectangle can break this).
Design patterns are reusable solutions; the GoF catalogued 23 in creational, structural and behavioural groups.
Singleton: private constructor + static access to one instance; beware thread safety and overuse.
Factory hides which concrete class is created; Observer notifies many listeners of changes.
Strategy swaps interchangeable algorithms through an interface using composition.
lessons.tip: Before coding any project, spend ten minutes drawing a UML class diagram on paper. Fixing a box and arrow costs nothing; fixing a built class hierarchy costs days.
lessons.task: Draw a UML class diagram for a food delivery app with Customer, Order, OrderItem, Restaurant, Rider and a PaymentGateway interface. Mark visibility, multiplicities and the right diamonds and triangles.

quiz.q: In UML, what does a filled black diamond mean?
quiz.explain: Filled diamond = composition; hollow diamond = aggregation.

quiz.q: Which SOLID principle says a class should have only one reason to change?
quiz.explain: S stands for Single Responsibility.

quiz.q: Which pattern ensures only one instance of a class exists?
quiz.explain: Singleton uses a private constructor and a static accessor.

quiz.q: Java's ActionListener mechanism is an example of which pattern?
quiz.explain: The button (subject) notifies registered listeners (observers).
